86205.q: What is a hill of sand piled up by the wind called?
86205.e: The wind carries grains of sand and drops them where it gets weaker. That is how a dune grows.
86205.m: A dune is a sand hill built by the wind.

86206.q: Which side of a dune is usually steeper?
a: The side facing away from the wind
The side the wind comes from
Both sides are always equally steep
86206.e: The wind pushes the sand up the gentle side. Behind the ridge, the sand slides down and forms a steep slope.
86206.m: A dune is steep on the side away from the wind.

a: Yes, the wind pushes them along
No, they always stay in place
86207.e: The wind blows sand over the dune. So it slowly moves on. It is then called a moving dune.
86207.m: Moving dunes slowly travel with the wind.

86208.q: Which plant holds the sand of the dunes in place on the North Sea?
86208.e: Marram grass has very long roots. With them it holds the sand so the wind cannot carry it away.
86208.m: Marram grass holds dunes in place.

86209.q: In which country is the Dune of Pilat, the highest moving dune in Europe?
86209.e: The Dune of Pilat lies on the Atlantic coast of France. It is about 100 metres high.
86209.m: Europe’s highest dune is in France.

86210.q: Why should you not walk all over the dunes on the coast?
a: Otherwise the plants that hold the sand get damaged
Because the sand is too hot
86210.e: If the plants are trampled, the wind can blow the dune away. Dunes protect the land from the sea.
86210.m: Staying on the paths protects the dunes.

86211.q: What is a dune shaped like a half-moon called?
86211.e: A crescent dune has two tips pointing with the wind. It looks like a crescent moon.
86211.m: A crescent dune is shaped like a half-moon.

86212.q: What can some dunes do when sand slides down them?
86212.e: When a lot of sand slides, the grains rub against each other. This makes a deep humming sound. People speak of singing dunes.
86212.m: There are dunes that can hum.

86213.q: In which large desert in Africa are there huge sand dunes?
86213.e: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. In some parts there are huge fields of dunes.
86213.m: There are huge dunes in the Sahara.

86214.q: What is the largest island in Lake Zurich called?
86214.e: Ufenau lies in Lake Zurich and belongs to the canton of Schwyz. You reach it by boat, because there is no bridge.
86214.m: Ufenau is an island in Lake Zurich.

86215.q: What do you call a group of many islands close together?
86215.e: An archipelago is a group of islands. One example is the many islands of Greece.
86215.m: Many islands together form an archipelago.

86216.q: What is a ring-shaped island made of coral called?
86216.e: An atoll is a ring of coral. In its middle there is an area of water.
86216.m: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral island.

86217.q: Which country in northern Europe is a large volcanic island in the Atlantic?
86217.e: Iceland lies in the North Atlantic and has many volcanoes and hot springs.
86217.m: Iceland is a volcanic island in the north.

86218.q: On which islands in the Pacific do famous giant tortoises live?
86218.e: Giant tortoises that can live for more than 100 years live on the Galápagos Islands.
86218.m: Giant tortoises live on the Galápagos Islands.

86219.e: When waves hit the coast, they break and foam. This is called surf.
86219.m: Surf forms when waves break on the coast.

86220.q: Why do waves break near the shore?
86220.e: In shallow water, the bottom of the wave is slowed down. The top is faster, tips forward and breaks.
86220.m: In shallow water, waves tip over and break.

86221.q: Why does the foam of the surf look white?
a: Because it contains lots of tiny air bubbles
Because there is soap in the sea
86221.e: When the wave breaks, a lot of air is mixed into the water. The many bubbles make the foam look white.
86221.m: Air bubbles make the foam white.

86222.q: What are the fine drops of water that splash into the air from the surf called?
86222.e: When waves crash against rocks, fine drops splash up. This is called spray.
86222.m: Water splashed up by the surf is called spray.

86223.q: What is a dangerous current that pulls water from the beach back out to sea called?
86223.e: The water of the surf flows back out to sea quickly in narrow channels. This rip current can pull swimmers out.
86223.m: A rip current pulls away from the beach out to sea.

86224.q: What should you do if a current pulls you away from the beach?
a: Swim sideways, parallel to the beach
Swim against the current with all your strength
86224.e: The current is usually only narrow. If you swim out sideways, you get out of it and can then get back to the shore.
86224.m: In a current, swim sideways along the beach.

86225.q: What does the surf do to sharp-edged stones over a long time?
86225.e: The waves roll the stones back and forth again and again. This grinds off the edges.

86226.q: When is the surf especially wild?
86226.e: A storm makes high waves. When they crash against the coast, the surf roars especially loudly.
86226.m: In a storm, the surf roars.

86228.q: Near which town in England are there famous white chalk cliffs?
86228.e: The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk. You can see them from a ship from far away.
86228.m: White chalk cliffs shine at Dover.

86229.q: On which German island in the Baltic Sea are there white chalk cliffs?
86229.e: On the island of Rügen, pale chalk cliffs rise steeply above the Baltic Sea. They are very well known.
86229.m: Rügen is famous for its chalk cliffs.

a: The waves wear away the rock until it breaks off
86230.e: The waves hollow out the rock at the bottom. At some point the upper part breaks off, and a steep wall forms.
86230.m: The waves eat into the rock and shape cliffs.

86231.q: Which seabird with a colourful beak nests on cliffs in the north?
86231.e: Puffins have an orange-striped beak. They nest in burrows on steep coasts, for example in Iceland.
86231.m: The puffin nests on steep coasts.

86232.q: What is a rock arch that the sea has washed out of a cliff called?
86232.e: The waves wash a hole through a rocky headland. What is left is an arch that the sea flows through.
86232.m: The sea can wash arches into the rocks.

86233.q: What is a single pillar of rock standing in the sea in front of a cliff called?
86233.e: When a sea arch collapses, a single pillar is often left standing in the sea.
86233.m: A sea stack stands alone in front of the coast.

86234.q: Why should you not go right to the edge of a cliff?
86234.e: The sea hollows out the rocks from below. So the edge can suddenly break off.
86234.m: Keep your distance from the edge of a cliff.

86235.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in seawater. Streams, rain and mountain lakes, on the other hand, have fresh water.

86236.q: Can you drink seawater when you are thirsty?
a: No, it makes you even thirstier
Yes, as much as you like
86236.e: All the salt draws water out of the body. Anyone who drinks seawater gets even thirstier.

86237.q: In which lake is the water so salty that you almost float on top by yourself?
86237.e: The Dead Sea is much saltier than the ocean. The heavy salt water carries your body like an air mattress.
86237.m: In the Dead Sea you hardly sink.

86238.q: Why is it easier to float in the sea than in a Swiss lake?
a: There are waves in the sea
The water in the lake is deeper
86238.e: Salt water is heavier than fresh water. So it pushes the body upwards more strongly.
86238.m: Salt water carries you better than fresh water.

a: Seawater is left to evaporate in the sun
It is dug up on the beach
It is collected from the seabed
86239.e: In shallow pools, the water evaporates in the sun. The salt is left over and is raked together.
86239.m: Sea salt is left over when seawater evaporates.

86240.q: The salt in Switzerland comes from the ground. How did it form long ago?
a: From an ancient sea that dried up
86240.e: More than 200 million years ago there was a sea here. When it dried up, the salt was left behind and later covered over.
86240.m: Swiss salt comes from an ancient sea.

86241.q: What do you call water with very little salt, like in lakes and rivers?
86241.e: The water in streams, rivers and most lakes contains hardly any salt. It is called fresh water.
86241.m: Lakes and rivers have fresh water.

86242.q: Where is the deepest point of all the oceans?
86242.e: The Mariana Trench is in the Pacific. The seabed there is deeper than anywhere else.
86242.m: The deepest point of the oceans is in the Mariana Trench.

86243.q: Roughly how deep is the deepest point in the ocean?
86243.e: The deepest point is almost 11,000 metres below sea level. Mount Everest would fit inside it.
86243.m: The deepest point of the ocean is about 11,000 metres deep.

86244.q: What is it like on the seabed of the deep sea?
86244.e: Sunlight only reaches a few hundred metres down into the water. Below that it is completely dark.
86244.m: The deep sea is pitch dark.

86245.q: What is there on the seabed?
86245.e: The seabed is very varied. There are huge mountain ranges, deep trenches and volcanoes.
86245.m: There are mountains and valleys under the sea too.

86246.q: Which Swiss man was one of the first people to dive into the Mariana Trench in 1960?
86246.e: In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived in the submersible Trieste to the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
86246.m: Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point of the ocean in 1960.

86247.q: Which deep-sea fish lures prey with a glowing bait?
86247.e: The anglerfish has a kind of fishing rod with a light on its head. Small animals swim towards the light and get eaten.
86247.m: The anglerfish catches prey with light.

86248.q: What do corals build on the seabed in warm seas?
86248.e: Corals are small animals with a limestone skeleton. Together they build large reefs over a long time.

86249.q: What is it like right at the bottom of the seabed?
86249.e: Sunlight only gets a little way into the water. Right at the bottom of the seabed it is pitch dark.
86249.m: Deep down in the sea it is dark.

86250.q: Why does a submersible for the deep sea need very thick walls?
a: The water presses very hard down there
There are rocks in the water there
86250.e: The deeper you dive, the more water presses down from above. In the deep sea this pressure is enormous.
86250.m: In the depths the water presses very hard.

86251.q: What is a shallow body of water on the coast that is almost cut off from the sea called?
86251.e: A lagoon is a shallow basin of seawater. It is connected to the sea only by narrow openings.
86251.m: A lagoon is almost cut off from the sea.

86252.q: Which famous city in Italy was built in a lagoon?
86252.e: Venice stands on many small islands in a lagoon. Instead of streets there are many canals.

86253.q: Which boat is typical of the canals in Venice?
86253.e: The black gondola is steered by a gondolier with an oar. It belongs to Venice.
86253.m: The gondola is the typical boat of Venice.

86254.q: What colour is the water in a South Sea lagoon often?
86254.e: The water in the lagoon is shallow and clear. Over the pale sand it shines turquoise blue.
86254.m: South Sea lagoons shine turquoise blue.

86255.q: Why is the water in a lagoon often warmer than in the open sea?
a: Because it is shallow and the sun warms it
Because there are hot springs in it
86255.e: Shallow water is warmed up quickly by the sun. That is why a lagoon is often pleasantly warm.

86256.q: In which country is the famous “Blue Lagoon”, a warm pool of thermal water?
86256.e: The Blue Lagoon in Iceland is fed by warm water from deep underground. It shines a milky blue.
86256.m: The Blue Lagoon is in Iceland.

86257.q: Which pink birds are often seen in lagoons by the Mediterranean?
86257.e: Flamingos stand in shallow water and eat small shrimps. That is where they get their pink colour.
86257.m: Flamingos like living in shallow lagoons.

86258.q: What often separates a lagoon from the open sea?
86258.e: Waves and currents deposit sand. This creates a narrow strip that shields the lagoon.
86258.m: A strip of sand protects the lagoon from the sea.

86259.q: Which country is especially famous for its fjords?
86259.e: The coast of Norway has more than a thousand fjords. Many people travel there to see them.
86259.m: Norway is the land of fjords.

86260.q: What carved out the deep valleys of the fjords long ago?
86260.e: In the Ice Age, huge glaciers scraped out deep valleys. Later the sea flowed in.

86261.q: What is the longest fjord in Norway called?
86261.e: The Sognefjord is about 200 km long. It reaches far inland.
86261.m: The Sognefjord is Norway’s longest fjord.

86262.q: In which country are there especially many fjords?
86262.e: Norway’s coast is cut by many fjords. The Geirangerfjord is even a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
86262.m: Norway is the land of fjords.

86263.q: Which other country also has many fjords?
86263.e: In the south of New Zealand, glaciers also shaped fjords. There they are often called “sounds”.

86264.q: What kind of water is in a fjord?
86264.e: A fjord is an arm of the sea. So it contains salt water, often mixed at the top with some fresh water from rivers.

a: No, a fjord is connected to the sea
Yes, it is the longest fjord
86265.e: Lake Lucerne is a freshwater lake. A real fjord is an arm of the sea.
86265.m: A fjord always belongs to the sea.

a: A mound of sand in shallow water
A wooden bench on the beach
86266.e: A sandbank is a deposit of sand in the sea or a river. It lies just below or above the water.
86266.m: A sandbank lies in shallow water.

86267.q: Why are sandbanks dangerous for ships?
a: Ships can run aground on them
86267.e: Because the water over a sandbank is shallow, a ship can get stuck. This is called running aground.
86267.m: Ships have to steer around sandbanks.

86268.q: When do many sandbanks in the North Sea appear above the water?
86268.e: At low tide, the sea draws back. Then many sandbanks come to the surface.

86269.q: Which animals like to rest on sandbanks in the North Sea?
86269.e: Seals lie on sandbanks in the sun and rest. At high tide they go back into the water.

86270.q: What shows ships where a sandbank is?
86270.e: Floating buoys mark dangerous places in the water. That way captains know where they can sail.

86271.q: Does a sandbank always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, it is glued to the bottom
No, it floats like a boat
86271.e: Currents and waves carry sand away and deposit it elsewhere. So sandbanks slowly move.

86272.q: How deep is the water over a sandbank?
a: As deep as a house is tall
86272.e: A sandbank is a hill of sand under water. So the water over it is very shallow.
86272.m: The water over a sandbank is shallow.

86273.q: Which gas makes party balloons float upwards?
86273.e: Helium is much lighter than air. That is why a balloon filled with helium floats upwards.
86273.m: A helium balloon rises because helium is lighter than air.

86274.q: What happens to a helium balloon after a few days?
86274.e: The helium slowly escapes through the skin of the balloon. That is why the balloon gets smaller and sinks to the ground.
86274.m: A helium balloon loses its gas over time.

86275.e: Helium is a noble gas and does not burn. That is why it is safe for balloons.
86275.m: Helium does not burn, so it is safe.

86276.q: Which object in the sky is helium named after?
86276.e: Helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun. ‘Helios’ is the Greek word for sun.
86276.m: Helium gets its name from the Sun.

86277.e: Helium is an invisible gas. You cannot see it.

86278.q: Why should you not breathe in helium from balloons?
a: You do not get enough oxygen
Your voice stays high for ever
86278.e: If you breathe in helium, not enough oxygen gets into your lungs. You can faint, and that is dangerous.
86278.m: Do not breathe in helium from balloons.

86279.q: What are modern airships filled with?
86279.e: Modern airships are filled with helium. It is light and does not burn.

86280.q: Which gas is the second lightest after hydrogen?
86280.e: Hydrogen is the lightest element. Helium comes straight after it.
86280.m: Helium is the second lightest element.

86281.e: Helium has no smell and no taste.

86282.q: What colour does neon glow in a tube light?
86282.e: When electricity flows through neon, it glows reddish orange. Other colours come from other gases or coloured tubes.

86283.q: What is neon at room temperature?
86283.e: Neon is a gas. You cannot see it at room temperature.

86284.q: Where is neon gas obtained from?
86284.e: There is a tiny amount of neon in the air. It is obtained by cooling air down a lot and separating it.
86284.m: Neon is obtained from the air.

86285.q: What does the name neon mean?
86285.e: ‘Neos’ means ‘new’ in Greek. Neon was newly discovered in 1898.
86285.m: The name neon means ‘the new one’.

86286.q: Which group of substances does neon belong to?
86286.e: Neon is a noble gas, like helium and argon. Noble gases hardly combine with other substances.
86286.m: Neon is one of the noble gases.

86287.e: Neon colours are loud and glowing, for example neon yellow. They are called that because they remind people of glowing neon tubes.
86287.m: Neon colours are bright and glowing.

86288.q: What are glowing advertising signs made of gas tubes called?
86288.e: Glowing writing made of bent glass tubes is called a neon sign. You see them on shops and cinemas.
86288.m: Neon signs glow in glass tubes.

a: Yes, even just looking at it
86289.e: Neon is not poisonous. It hardly reacts with other substances.

86290.q: What does a B on a pencil mean?
86290.e: B stands for ‘black’. A B pencil contains a lot of graphite and writes soft and dark.
86290.m: A B pencil writes soft and dark.

86291.q: What can you use to lubricate a sticking door lock?
86291.e: Graphite is smooth and lubricates without being sticky. That is why fine graphite powder helps with sticking locks.
86291.m: Graphite powder makes locks turn more easily.

86292.q: Why can you rub out pencil lines?
a: The graphite only lies on top of the paper
The line is made of water
86292.e: When you write, tiny bits of graphite stay on the paper. The rubber picks them up again.
86292.m: You can rub out pencil because the graphite only sits on top.

86293.e: Graphite is greyish black and a little shiny. That is why a pencil writes grey.

86294.e: The layers in graphite slide easily over each other. That is why it feels smooth and greasy.

86295.e: Graphite conducts electricity even though it is not a metal. That is why it is used in batteries, for example.

86296.q: Why is the core of a pencil called ‘lead’?
a: People used to think graphite was lead
It is as heavy as lead
Its casing used to be made of lead
86296.e: In the past, people thought graphite was a kind of lead. The name stuck, even though there is no lead in it.
86296.m: There is no lead in a pencil.

86297.q: What does the Greek word that ‘graphite’ comes from mean?
86297.e: ‘Graphein’ means ‘to write’ in Greek. You can write with graphite.
86297.m: Graphite comes from the Greek word for ‘to write’.

86298.q: Why is chlorine added to swimming pool water?
86298.e: Chlorine kills bacteria and other germs. That keeps the pool water clean.

86299.q: When does an indoor pool smell especially strongly of ‘chlorine’?
a: When there is a lot of sweat in the water
When the water is completely clean
When the sun is shining outside
When only a few people are swimming
86299.e: The typical pool smell forms when chlorine reacts with sweat, wee and dirt. That is why you shower before swimming.
86299.m: Showering before swimming helps against the chlorine smell.

86300.e: Pure chlorine is yellowish green. Its name comes from the Greek word for ‘yellowish green’.

86301.q: Which element is found together with sodium in table salt?
86301.e: The chemical name for table salt is sodium chloride. It is made of sodium and chlorine.
86301.m: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine.

86302.q: What protects your eyes from chlorinated water when swimming?
86302.e: Chlorinated water can irritate the eyes. Swimming goggles keep the water away from your eyes.
86302.m: Swimming goggles protect your eyes in the pool.

86303.e: Pure chlorine is very poisonous. But in a swimming pool there is only a tiny amount of chlorine in the water.

86304.q: What can chlorinated water do to colourful swimwear?
86304.e: Chlorine bleaches colours. That is why swimwear gets paler over time.

86305.q: What is chlorine at room temperature?
86305.e: Pure chlorine is a gas at room temperature. It is heavier than air.

86306.q: What is fluoride in toothpaste good for?
86306.e: Fluoride makes tooth enamel harder. That way teeth do not get holes so quickly.

86307.q: About how much toothpaste do small children need?
86307.e: For small children, an amount the size of a pea is enough. That is enough to protect the teeth.
86307.m: Small children only need a pea-sized amount of toothpaste.

86308.q: What do you do with the toothpaste foam after brushing your teeth?
86308.e: You do not swallow toothpaste. You spit out the foam.

86309.q: Which food can you also buy with fluoride in Switzerland?
86309.e: In Switzerland there is table salt with iodine and fluoride. It helps to protect teeth.
86309.m: In Switzerland there is salt with fluoride.

86310.q: Which thing that you use every day contains fluoride?
86310.e: Fluoride in toothpaste makes teeth stronger. That is why you brush them with toothpaste.

86311.q: Which drink naturally contains quite a lot of fluoride?
86311.e: Tea plants take up fluoride from the soil. That is why black tea contains quite a lot of it.

86312.q: What is pure fluorine at room temperature?
86312.e: Pure fluorine is a pale yellow gas. It is very poisonous and reacts violently.
86312.m: Pure fluorine is a poisonous gas.

86313.q: What forms as a white layer in the kettle?
86313.e: Tap water contains dissolved lime. When it boils, the lime is left behind as a white layer.
86313.m: Limescale forms white crusts in the kettle.

86314.q: Which animals build huge reefs of lime in the sea?
86314.e: Corals are tiny animals. They build skeletons of lime, and these grow into large reefs.
86314.m: Coral reefs are made of lime.

86315.q: Which rock are the Jura mountains mostly made of?
86315.e: The Jura is mostly made of limestone. It formed long ago at the bottom of a sea.
86315.m: The Jura is made of limestone.

86316.q: What are seashells and snail shells made of?
86316.e: Mussels and snails build their shells from lime. They take the lime from the water or from their food.
86316.m: Mussels build their shells from lime.

86317.q: What is the shell of a hen's egg mainly made of?
86317.e: Eggshells are almost entirely made of lime. The hen needs a lot of lime from its food for this.

86318.q: What are stalactites and stalagmites in caves made of?
86318.e: Water with dissolved lime drips from the cave ceiling. The lime is left behind and grows very slowly into stalactites and stalagmites.
86318.m: Stalactites and stalagmites grow from lime.

86319.q: What is tap water with a lot of lime in it called?
86319.e: Water with a lot of lime is called hard water. Water with little lime is called soft water.
86319.m: Water with a lot of lime is called hard.

86320.q: What happens when you drip vinegar onto a piece of limestone?
86320.e: Vinegar is an acid and reacts with lime. A gas forms, and it fizzes.
86320.m: Limestone fizzes when vinegar touches it.

86321.q: Which gas forms when lime reacts with acid?
86321.e: Lime contains carbon and oxygen. With acid, it produces the gas carbon dioxide.
86321.m: Lime and acid give carbon dioxide.

86322.e: Pure sulphur is light yellow. It is found as yellow crystals.

86323.q: What do many substances containing sulphur smell of?
86323.e: Hydrogen sulphide smells of rotten eggs. Pure sulphur itself hardly smells.
86323.m: Some sulphur substances stink of rotten eggs.

86324.q: Where is sulphur often found in nature?
86324.e: Gases containing sulphur come out of volcanoes. Yellow sulphur settles there.
86324.m: Yellow sulphur is found at volcanoes.

86325.q: What is in the head of many matches?
86325.e: The head of many matches contains sulphur. It helps the wood catch fire.

86326.q: Is pure sulphur solid, liquid or a gas at room temperature?
86326.e: Pure sulphur is a solid. It only melts at about 115 degrees.

86327.q: In which town in the canton of Aargau does warm thermal water containing sulphur bubble up?
86327.e: In Baden, warm water comes out of the ground. It contains sulphur and many other minerals.
86327.m: Baden has thermal water containing sulphur.

86328.q: What colour flame does sulphur burn with?
86328.e: Sulphur burns with a blue flame. A gas with a sharp smell forms.

86329.q: Which letter is the symbol for sulphur?
86329.e: Sulphur is called ‘sulfur’ in Latin. That is why its symbol is S.
86329.m: The symbol for sulphur is S.

86330.e: Liquid nitrogen looks like water. But it is extremely cold and evaporates at once.

86331.q: Roughly how much of the air is nitrogen?
86331.e: Around 78 out of 100 parts of the air are nitrogen. That is about three quarters.
86331.m: About three quarters of the air is nitrogen.

86332.q: About how cold is liquid nitrogen?
86332.e: Nitrogen only becomes liquid at about minus 196 degrees. So it is extremely cold.

86333.q: Why does garden fertiliser often contain nitrogen?
a: So that the soil stays dry
86333.e: Plants need nitrogen to build leaves and stems. That is why fertiliser often contains nitrogen.

86334.q: What does our body do with the nitrogen from the air when we breathe?
86334.e: Our body does not need the nitrogen from the air. We simply breathe it out again.
86334.m: We breathe the nitrogen from the air out again.

86336.q: Which gas is often put in crisp packets to keep the crisps fresh?
86336.e: Nitrogen pushes the oxygen out of the packet. That way the crisps do not go stale so quickly.

86337.q: Which letter is the symbol for nitrogen?
86337.e: Nitrogen is called ‘nitrogenium’ in Latin. That is why its symbol is N.
86337.m: The symbol for nitrogen is N.

86338.q: What happens to a flower dipped in liquid nitrogen?
a: It bursts into bloom at once
86338.e: Liquid nitrogen is so cold that the flower freezes instantly. After that it shatters like glass.
86338.m: Liquid nitrogen makes flowers rock hard.

86339.q: What happens to an iron screw placed on mercury?
86339.e: Mercury is almost twice as heavy as iron. That is why iron floats on mercury like wood on water.

86340.e: Mercury shines silver like a mirror. That is why its old name is quicksilver.

86341.q: Which measuring device often used to contain mercury?
86341.e: In the past, mercury in a clinical thermometer showed your temperature. Today other thermometers are used.
86341.m: Clinical thermometers used to contain mercury.

86342.e: Mercury and its vapour are poisonous. That is why it is replaced wherever possible today.

86343.q: What do you do if an old mercury thermometer breaks?
a: Touch nothing and fetch an adult
Pick it up with your fingers
86343.e: Mercury is poisonous, so you do not touch it. Adults must get rid of it carefully.
86343.m: Do not touch mercury from a broken thermometer.

86344.q: Which planet has the same name as the metal mercury?
86344.e: In English the metal and the planet are both called mercury. In German, however, the metal is called Quecksilber.
86344.m: The metal mercury shares its name with the planet.

86346.q: What does mercury form when you pour it onto a table?
86346.e: Mercury pulls itself together into round beads. These roll around easily.

86347.q: What does our body need calcium for?
86347.e: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard and strong. Almost all the calcium in the body is in the bones.
86347.m: Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

86348.q: Which drink provides a lot of calcium?
86348.e: Milk contains a lot of calcium. One glass of milk already covers a good part of what you need in a day.
86348.m: Milk provides a lot of calcium.

86349.q: Which food contains a lot of calcium?
86349.e: Cheese contains a lot of calcium. Hard cheese such as Sbrinz has especially lots.
86349.m: Cheese contains a lot of calcium.

86350.e: Pure calcium is a soft, silvery metal. In nature, however, it is only found in compounds.

86351.q: Which green vegetable contains a lot of calcium?
86351.e: Broccoli and other green cabbage vegetables contain a lot of calcium. Cucumbers have only a little.

86352.q: What is the symbol for calcium?
86352.e: The symbol for calcium is Ca. C stands for carbon and Cl for chlorine.
86352.m: The symbol for calcium is Ca.

86353.q: Which vitamin helps the body take in calcium?
86353.e: Vitamin D helps calcium from food get into the bones. Our skin makes vitamin D in sunlight.
86353.m: Vitamin D helps the body take in calcium.

86354.q: What happens to bones if you do not get enough calcium?
86354.e: Without enough calcium, bones become weaker. They can then break more easily.
86354.m: Too little calcium makes bones brittle.

86355.q: Which illness used to be common in Switzerland because of a lack of iodine?
86355.e: Without enough iodine, a large swelling can form on the neck. This is called a goitre.
86355.m: Iodine in salt protects against goitre.

86356.e: The thyroid gland sits at the front of the neck. It needs iodine to make important messenger substances.

86357.q: Which country was among the first to have iodised salt in 1922?
86357.e: In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce iodised salt. After that, illnesses caused by a lack of iodine became much rarer.
86357.m: Switzerland has had iodised salt since 1922.

86358.q: Which food naturally contains a lot of iodine?
86358.e: There is a lot of iodine in the sea. That is why sea fish and seaweed contain a lot of it.
86358.m: Sea fish contains a lot of iodine.

86359.q: Why does Swiss soil contain little iodine?
a: Glaciers and rain washed it away
86359.e: During the Ice Age and through rain, the iodine was washed out of the soil. That is why vegetables from Switzerland contain little iodine.
86359.m: Swiss soil is poor in iodine.

86360.q: What colour is the vapour of heated iodine?
86360.e: Heated iodine forms a violet vapour. The name iodine comes from the Greek word for ‘violet coloured’.

86361.q: What was tincture of iodine used for in the past?
86361.e: Tincture of iodine kills germs. In the past it was painted onto wounds.

86362.q: What colour does a potato turn when you drip iodine solution on it?
86362.e: Iodine turns starch bluish black. Potatoes contain a lot of starch.

86363.e: Pure gold shines yellow. That is why this colour is also called ‘golden’.

86364.e: Gold hardly combines with air and water. That is why it does not rust and stays shiny for a long time.

86365.q: What is a rectangular block of pure gold called?
86365.e: Gold is often cast into bars. That makes it easy to store and weigh.
86365.m: A gold bar is a block of gold.

86366.q: In which area of Switzerland do people often pan for gold in streams?
86366.e: In the streams around the Napf you can find small flakes of gold. There are also gold panning courses there.
86366.m: You can pan for gold in the Napf area.

86367.q: What is gold beaten wafer-thin called?
86367.e: Gold is so soft that it can be beaten very thin. This gold leaf is thinner than a hair.

86368.e: The Swiss National Bank owns Switzerland's gold reserves. A large part of it is kept in Switzerland.
86368.m: The National Bank looks after Switzerland's gold.

86369.e: Gold is much heavier than most substances. That is why even a small cube of gold is surprisingly heavy.
86369.m: Gold is a very heavy metal.

86370.q: What is the well-known old Swiss gold coin called?
86370.e: The gold Vreneli was minted from 1897 to 1949. It shows a woman's head.
86370.m: The Vreneli is a Swiss gold coin.

86567.q: What is the first page of a website, which you usually see first, called?
86567.e: The home page is like the front door of a website. From there you get to the other pages.
86567.m: Every website has a home page.

86568.q: What is a website usually made of?
86568.e: A website is a collection of many web pages. They belong together, like the pages in a book.
86568.m: A website is made up of several web pages.

86569.q: What do you do if a web page is longer than your screen?
86569.e: With the mouse wheel or your finger you push the page up. That way you see the part further down.
86569.m: By scrolling you see the rest of a long page.

86570.q: What do you often find at the very top of a website to get to the different pages?
86570.e: The menu shows the most important pages of the website. You click on a word and get to that page.
86570.m: The menu helps you find your way around a website.

86571.e: People write the texts, choose pictures and build the pages. Companies, schools and even children can make websites.
86571.m: There are people behind every website.

86572.q: Apart from text, what else can often be seen on many websites?
86572.e: Websites do not only show words. Often there are also photos, drawings and videos.
86572.m: Websites have texts, pictures and videos.

86573.q: What can happen when nobody looks after a website any more?
a: The information gets out of date.
86573.e: Websites need looking after. If nobody updates them, dates and details are often no longer right.
86573.m: Information on old websites can be out of date.

86574.q: What should you do if a website asks you to buy something?
86574.e: Buying costs real money. That is why children always ask an adult first.
86574.m: Before buying anything online, you ask your parents.

86575.q: What does a small magnifying glass symbol on a website often show?
86575.e: The magnifying glass stands for searching. There you can type in a word and search for it on the website.
86575.m: The magnifying glass on a website stands for search.

86576.q: Which of these programs is a web browser?
86576.e: Firefox is a browser for looking at web pages. Word is for writing and Paint is for drawing.

86577.q: Which button in the browser takes you to the previous page?
86577.e: The arrow pointing left takes you back one page. The arrow pointing right goes forward again.
86577.m: The back arrow takes you to the last page.

86578.q: Where do you type a web address in the browser?
86578.e: The address bar is the long box at the top of the browser. There you type in the address and press Enter.
86578.m: You type web addresses into the address bar.

86579.q: What are the little labels at the top of the browser called, which let you have several pages open at once?
86579.e: Each tab is like a separate sheet in the browser. You can switch between tabs with one click.
86579.m: With tabs you can have several pages open.

86580.q: How can you save a favourite page in the browser?
86580.e: A bookmark saves the address of a page. Later you find the page again with one click. Often there is a star for this.
86580.m: With a bookmark you find pages again quickly.

86581.q: What does the circular arrow in the browser do?
86581.e: The circular arrow is called “Reload” or “Refresh”. The page is then loaded again.
86581.m: With the circular arrow you reload a page.

86582.q: What do you mainly need a web browser for?
86582.e: The web browser fetches web pages from the internet and shows them. Without a browser you cannot see web pages.
86582.m: A web browser shows web pages.

86583.q: What does a small padlock next to the web address in the browser show?
86583.e: The padlock means that the data is protected on its way. But it does not automatically mean that the page is good.
86583.m: The padlock shows a protected connection.

86584.q: Which program on an iPad is a web browser?
86584.e: Safari is the browser that comes with iPads and iPhones. With the camera, on the other hand, you take photos.

86585.q: What is a hyperlink often called for short?
86585.e: Instead of hyperlink, people usually just say link. Both mean the same.
86585.m: A hyperlink is called a link for short.

86586.q: What happens when you click on a link?
86586.e: A link takes you to another page or another place. That is why the browser jumps there.
86586.m: A link takes you to another page.

86587.q: What shape does the mouse pointer often take when it is over a link?
86587.e: Over a link, the arrow often turns into a small hand with a pointing finger. That way you know you can click there.
86587.m: The small hand shows you a link.

86588.q: What do text links on web pages often look like?
86588.e: Many websites show links in blue with a line underneath. But some pages design links differently.
86588.m: Blue, underlined words are often links.

86589.q: Can a picture be a link too?
86589.e: Pictures and buttons can be links too. If you click on them, another page opens.

86590.q: What should you do with a link in a message from a stranger?
86590.e: Links from strangers can lead to dangerous pages. Better to ask an adult.
86590.m: I do not click on links from strangers.

86591.q: Why is the web called a “web”?
a: Because it is made of string
86591.e: Countless links connect the web pages with each other. That makes a web, like a spider's web.
86591.m: Links connect web pages into a web.

86592.q: What do you usually tap a link with on a tablet?
86592.e: On a tablet or phone you tap the link with your finger. On a computer you usually use the mouse.
86592.m: On a tablet you tap links with your finger.

86593.q: Which three letters do many web addresses begin with?
86593.e: Many addresses begin with www, for example www.sbb.ch. But some addresses also work without www.
86593.m: Many web addresses begin with www.

86594.q: Which character separates the parts of a web address like www.sbb.ch?
86594.e: In a web address there are dots between the parts. You say, for example, “www dot sbb dot ch”.
86594.m: In web addresses there are dots between the parts.

86595.q: What usually happens if you make a typing mistake in a web address?
a: You end up on the wrong page.
86595.e: The computer looks for exactly the address you type. If one letter is wrong, you get an error message or a different page.
86595.m: You must type web addresses exactly right.

86596.q: Can a web address contain a space?
86596.e: Web addresses have no spaces. Instead of a space there is sometimes a hyphen.
86596.m: Web addresses are written without spaces.

86597.q: How many times does the same web address exist on the whole internet?
86597.e: Every web address is unique, like a home address. That way the computer always finds the right page.
86597.m: Each web address exists only once.

86598.q: Which ending do many web addresses from Switzerland have?
86598.e: The ending .ch comes from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica. The federal government uses it too, for example in admin.ch.
86598.m: Swiss web addresses often end in .ch.

86599.q: What do web addresses with a protected connection begin with?
86599.e: The s at the end of https stands for “secure”. The data is then sent encrypted.
86599.m: With https the connection is protected.

86600.q: What did the ending .com in a web address originally stand for?
86600.e: .com comes from the word “commercial” and was meant for companies. Today, though, many different websites use it.
86600.m: The ending .com was originally meant for companies.

86601.q: What is it called when you copy a file from the internet onto your device?
86601.e: Getting a file from the internet is a download. Upload is the opposite, sending a file to the internet.
86601.m: Getting a file from the internet is called downloading.

86602.q: What happens when you download a file?
a: It is saved on your device.
86602.e: When downloading, your device fetches a file from the internet. After that it is saved on your device.
86602.m: What you download is then on your device.

86603.q: What is the opposite of downloading?
86603.e: When uploading, you send a file from your device to the internet. When downloading, you fetch it from the internet.
86603.m: Uploading is the opposite of downloading.

86604.q: Which symbol often stands for downloading?
86604.e: An arrow pointing down shows that something is coming from the internet onto your device. An arrow pointing up often stands for uploading.
86604.m: An arrow pointing down means downloading.

86605.q: What takes the longest to download?
86605.e: A film is a very big file. The bigger a file is, the longer it takes to download.
86605.m: Big files take longer to download.

86606.q: Who do you ask before you download something?
a: A child you do not know in a chat
86606.e: Some files can be dangerous or cost money. That is why children ask an adult first.
86606.m: Before downloading, you ask an adult.

86607.q: In which folder do downloaded files often end up on a computer?
86607.e: Most computers save downloaded files in the “Downloads” folder. That is where you find them again.
86607.m: You often find downloaded files in the “Downloads” folder.

86608.q: What can a downloaded file from an unknown site contain?
86608.e: A computer virus is a harmful program. It can hide in files that you download.
86608.m: Files from unknown sites can contain viruses.

86609.q: Which word does the word “app” come from?
86609.e: App is short for “application”. That means a program you use.

86610.q: Where do you download new apps on a phone?
86610.e: An app store is a shop for apps on a phone or tablet. Some apps are free, others cost money.
86610.m: You get apps from an app store.

86611.q: What are the small pictures on the screen that you use to open an app called?
86611.e: Every app has a small picture called an icon. If you tap it, the app starts.
86611.m: You open an app by tapping its icon.

86612.q: What does an update do to an app?
86612.e: With an update the app is improved. Bugs are fixed and sometimes new things are added.
86612.m: An update makes an app better.

86613.q: Which app on a phone shows you what time it is?
86613.e: The clock app shows the time. Often it also has an alarm and a stopwatch.
86613.m: The clock app shows you the time.

86614.q: What can you do with an app that you no longer need?
86614.e: You can remove unnecessary apps from your device. That gives you more storage space again.
86614.m: You can delete apps you do not need.

86615.q: What do many apps need so that everything works?
86615.e: Many apps fetch data from the internet, for example weather or news. Without a connection that does not work.

86616.q: What does a weather app show?
a: What the weather will be like
86616.e: A weather app fetches weather data from the internet. It shows, for example, whether it is raining or the sun is shining.
86616.m: A weather app shows the weather.

86617.e: A server is a computer that delivers things to other computers, for example web pages or videos. The word comes from “to serve”.
86617.m: A server delivers data to other computers.

86618.q: When do most servers on the internet work?
86618.e: People all over the world need the internet at all times. That is why servers run without a break.

86619.q: What does a server deliver when you watch a video on the internet?
86619.e: The video is stored on a server. The server sends it to your device bit by bit.
86619.m: Videos on the internet come from servers.

86620.q: What does a server need to work?
86620.e: A server is a computer and needs electricity. That is why lots of servers use a lot of energy.

86621.q: Why are rooms with lots of servers cooled?
a: Because the servers want to feel cold
Because otherwise it is too loud
86621.e: Servers work hard and get hot doing it. They are cooled so that they do not break.
86621.m: Servers are cooled because they get warm.

86622.q: How many people can fetch data from a server at the same time?
86622.e: A server can answer lots of requests at the same time. That is why lots of people can look at the same page.
86622.m: A server serves lots of people at the same time.

86623.q: Where are your messages often stored before they reach your friend?
86623.e: When you send a message, it goes to a server first. From there it is sent on to your friend.

86624.q: What happens when a website's server breaks down?
86624.e: The website is on the server. If the server is broken or switched off, nobody can open the page.
86624.m: Without its server, a website cannot be reached.

86625.q: What does the router do at home?
a: It connects the devices to the internet.
86625.e: The router is the little box that connects your home to the internet. All devices send their data through it.
86625.m: The router brings the internet into your home.

86626.q: What does the router at home share with phones and tablets without a cable?
86626.e: Most routers send out Wi-Fi. Devices connect to it without a cable.
86626.m: The router sends out the Wi-Fi.

86627.q: What do the little lights on the router show?
86627.e: The lights show whether the router has power and is connected to the internet. If a light is red, there is often a problem.
86627.m: The lights on the router show whether everything is working.

86628.q: What often helps when the internet at home is not working?
86628.e: You switch the router off and on again after a short time. After that it often connects properly again.

86629.q: What can a router be compared to?
86629.e: The router sends data to the right address, like a postman delivers letters. That way every message reaches the right device.
86629.m: A router delivers data like a postman delivers letters.

86630.q: What do you need to connect to the router's Wi-Fi?
86630.e: Wi-Fi is usually protected with a password. Only people who know it can connect.
86630.m: Wi-Fi is protected with a password.

86631.q: What can you use to connect a computer to the router without Wi-Fi?
86631.e: You plug a network cable into the computer and the router. The connection through the cable is often faster and more stable than Wi-Fi.
86631.m: With a network cable you connect devices without Wi-Fi.

86632.q: Where in the flat is the Wi-Fi usually strongest?
a: Very far away from the router
86632.e: The signal comes from the router. The further away you are, the weaker it gets.
86632.m: The Wi-Fi is strongest close to the router.

86633.q: How many devices can be connected to a router at the same time?
86633.e: Phone, tablet, computer and television can all be connected to the router at the same time. The router shares the connection.
86633.m: A router connects several devices at the same time.

86634.e: Submarine cables lie on the floor of the sea. They connect countries and continents.
86634.m: Submarine cables lie on the seabed.

86635.e: Submarine cables run, for example, from Europe to America. That way the internet is connected all over the world.

86636.q: How does most internet data get from Europe to America?
86636.e: Almost all the data between continents travels through cables in the sea. Satellites carry only a small part.
86636.m: Most data between continents travels through submarine cables.

86637.q: What travels through the glass fibres in modern submarine cables?
86637.e: In the thin glass fibres, the data travels as light signals. Light is very fast.
86637.m: In fibre-optic cables data travels as light.

86638.q: What are submarine cables laid with?
86638.e: Cable layers are big ships with huge reels of cable. They slowly let the cable sink to the seabed.
86638.m: Special ships lay the submarine cables.

86639.q: What can damage a submarine cable?
86639.e: Anchors and fishing nets can damage submarine cables. Then a ship has to repair the cable.
86639.m: Anchors and fishing nets can damage submarine cables.

86640.q: How is Switzerland connected to the submarine cables?
86640.e: Switzerland is not by the sea. That is why cables run over land to the coasts, where the submarine cables begin.
86640.m: Switzerland is connected to the submarine cables by land cables.

86641.q: What was the first thing sent through a cable across the Atlantic more than 150 years ago?
86641.e: In 1858 the first cable was laid across the Atlantic. It carried telegrams, which are short messages. There was no internet back then.
86641.m: The first Atlantic cable carried telegrams.

86642.e: Online means that a device is connected to the internet. Then you can open web pages.
86642.m: When you are online, you are connected to the internet.

86643.e: Offline means that a device has no connection to the internet at the moment. The device can still be switched on.
86643.m: When you are offline, you are not connected to the internet.

86644.q: What happens to a phone when you switch on aeroplane mode?
86644.e: In aeroplane mode the phone switches off its wireless connections. That is why it is offline, but it stays switched on.
86644.m: In aeroplane mode the phone is offline.

86645.q: What can you do offline too?
86645.e: Photos on your device are already saved. You do not need the internet for that.

a: A game played over the internet
86646.e: In an online game you are connected to the internet. Often you play with other people.
86646.m: Online games are played over the internet.

86647.q: What is a good idea when you have been online for a long time?
86647.e: Breaks are good for your eyes and your body. Playing, being outside or reading work offline too.
86647.m: Breaks from the screen do you good.

86648.q: What often appears on the screen when a device has no internet connection?
86648.e: If the device is offline, the browser or app shows a message. Often it says “No connection”.
86648.m: The message “No connection” shows that you are offline.

86649.q: What are maps called that you save before a trip so they work without the internet?
86649.e: Offline maps are loaded onto the device beforehand. Then you do not need the internet on the way.
86649.m: Offline maps work without the internet.

86650.q: In a chat app, what does a green dot next to a name often show?
86650.e: Many apps use a green dot to show that someone is online right now. If the dot is missing, the person is usually offline.
86650.m: A green dot often shows that someone is online.

86651.q: Along with the web, what did Tim Berners-Lee invent for looking at web pages?
86651.e: In 1990 at CERN, Tim Berners-Lee programmed the first web browser himself. He called it WorldWideWeb.
86651.m: Tim Berners-Lee also wrote the first web browser.

86652.q: In which country is the research centre CERN, where Tim Berners-Lee invented the web?
86652.e: Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN near Geneva. That is where the World Wide Web was born.
86652.m: The web was invented at CERN near Geneva.

86653.q: Which country does Tim Berners-Lee come from?
86653.e: Tim Berners-Lee was born in London in 1955. He is English.

86654.q: What does the abbreviation www stand for?
86654.e: www means World Wide Web, a network that spans the world. Tim Berners-Lee invented it.

86655.q: How much money did Tim Berners-Lee ask for so that everyone could use the web?
86655.e: He wanted the web to belong to everyone. That is why the web is free for everyone to use.
86655.m: The web is a gift to everyone.

86656.q: In which year did the first website go online?
86656.e: The first website went online at CERN in 1991. It explained what the web is.
86656.m: The first website went online in 1991.

86657.q: Which title of honour did Tim Berners-Lee receive from the British Queen?
86657.e: The Queen knighted him in 2004. Since then he has been called Sir Tim Berners-Lee.
86657.m: Tim Berners-Lee has the title Sir.

86658.q: What did a note on the world's first web server say?
86658.e: Tim Berners-Lee's computer had a note stuck on it saying: this machine is a server, do not power it down! Otherwise the whole web would no longer have been reachable.
86658.m: The first web server was not allowed to be switched off.

86659.q: What is special about a search engine for children?
a: It is only open at night.
86659.e: Adults check the pages beforehand. That way the children's search engine only shows pages that are suitable for children.
86659.m: Children's search engines show checked pages.

86660.q: What is the list that a search engine shows after searching called?
86660.e: After searching, the search engine shows a list of matching pages. Each page in this list is a result.
86660.m: The search engine shows you a list of results.

86661.q: Which of these is a search engine for children?
86661.e: fragFINN is a search engine for children. It only finds checked pages.
86661.m: fragFINN is a search engine for children.

86662.q: What do you do to open a page you have found in the search engine?
86662.e: Every search result is a link. When you click or tap on it, the page opens.
86662.m: You open a search result with a click.

86663.q: What do you type into a children's search engine?
86663.e: You type in a word, for example “hedgehog”. Then the search engine shows matching pages.
86663.m: You type a search word into a search engine.

86664.q: What do you do if you find something strange in the children's search engine?
86664.e: Even a children's search engine is not perfect. Tell an adult if something seems strange to you.
86664.m: With strange pages, I fetch an adult.

86665.q: Compared with a normal search engine, how many results does a children's search engine usually show?
86665.e: Children's search engines only search selected pages. That is why there are fewer, but more suitable, results.
86665.m: Children's search engines show fewer but suitable results.

86666.q: Who checks the pages for a children's search engine?
86666.e: Experts look at the pages before they go on the list. That keeps unsuitable pages out.
86666.m: Experts check the pages for children's search engines.

87149.q: What do igneous rocks form from?
87149.e: Igneous rocks form when magma inside the Earth or lava at the surface cools and becomes solid. They are also called solidified rocks.
87149.m: Igneous rocks form when molten rock solidifies.

87150.q: What are igneous rocks that have solidified slowly deep in the Earth’s crust called?
87150.e: Plutonic rocks, also called intrusive rocks, cool very slowly deep below the surface. A well-known example is granite.
87150.m: Plutonic rocks solidify slowly deep in the Earth’s crust.

87151.q: What are igneous rocks that have solidified from lava at the Earth’s surface called?
87151.e: Extrusive rocks, also called volcanic rocks, form from lava that flows out during volcanic eruptions. They cool quickly.
87151.m: Extrusive rocks form from lava at the Earth’s surface.

87152.q: Why do plutonic rocks usually have large, clearly visible crystals?
a: They are polished by the wind
They contain a lot of water
87152.e: When molten rock cools slowly, the crystals have a lot of time to grow. That is why you can see the individual grains in granite clearly.
87152.m: Slow cooling lets large crystals grow.

87153.q: What is the black, glassy rock that forms when lava cools extremely quickly called?
87153.e: With very fast cooling, no crystals can form, and volcanic glass is created. Obsidian has sharp broken edges and was used for blades in the Stone Age.

87154.q: Which volcanic rock is so full of gas bubbles that it can float on water?
87154.e: Pumice forms from gas-rich lava that froths up during an eruption. The many holes make it so light that it floats.
87154.m: Pumice is so porous that it can float.

87155.q: Which mountain range is the volcanic rock andesite named after?
87155.e: Andesite is a grey extrusive rock that is very common in the volcanoes of the Andes in South America. That is where it gets its name.
87155.m: Andesite is named after the Andes in South America.

87156.q: Which dark extrusive rock makes up a large part of the seabed and volcanic islands such as Hawaii?
87156.e: Basalt forms from runny lava that solidifies quickly. It is dark, fine-grained and the most common volcanic rock on Earth.
87156.m: Basalt is a dark rock made of solidified lava.

a: From rock that is changed by heat
From metal that melts in the Earth’s core
87157.e: Sand, mud, gravel or shells are deposited in layers. Under the weight of new layers, they are pressed together and cemented.
87157.m: Sedimentary rocks form from deposited, hardened particles.

87158.q: What forms when loose sand is pressed together and cemented over a long time?
87158.e: New layers press down with their weight on the sand below. Water is squeezed out, and minerals cement the grains together. Over time, sand becomes sandstone.
87158.m: Pressed and cemented sand becomes sandstone.

87159.q: What can you often see clearly in sedimentary rocks in a rock face?
a: Layers lying on top of each other
87159.e: Sediments are deposited layer by layer. That is why sedimentary rocks often show clear layers, as you can see in the Jura, for example.
87159.m: Sedimentary rocks are often built up in clear layers.

87160.q: What is Nagelfluh, which you can see on the Rigi or in Toggenburg, for example?
a: A rock made of cemented pebbles
A rock made of solidified lava
A rock made of glacier ice
A rock made of pure salt
87160.e: Millions of years ago, rivers deposited lots of round pebbles. These were cemented together with sand and lime. The stones look like nail heads in a wall.
87160.m: Nagelfluh is made of cemented pebbles.

87161.e: When the water in a cut-off sea basin evaporates, the dissolved salt is left behind. Such salt deposits are found near Bex in Vaud, for example.
87161.m: Rock salt is left behind when seawater evaporates.

87162.q: Which sedimentary rock is made of the very finest particles?
87162.e: Clay particles are tiny and only settle in very still water. Once hardened, they form claystone.
87162.m: Claystone is made of the finest clay particles.

87163.q: What material did coal mainly form from?
87163.e: Millions of years ago, huge amounts of dead plants piled up in swamps. Without air, under pressure and heat, they turned into peat and then coal.
87163.m: Coal is a sedimentary rock made of ancient plant remains.

87164.q: Which sedimentary rock makes up a large part of the Jura mountains?
87164.e: In the Jura, lime mud and shells were deposited in a warm sea. This became limestone, which was later folded up into mountains.
87164.m: The Jura is mostly made of limestone.

87165.q: Roughly what share of the Earth’s land surface is covered by sedimentary rocks?
87165.e: Sedimentary rocks form only a thin skin on the Earth’s crust. But this skin covers about three quarters of the land surface.
87165.m: Sedimentary rocks cover about three quarters of the land.

a: By being changed under high pressure and high temperature
By being deposited in a lake
87166.e: When a rock gets deep into the Earth, pressure and heat change its minerals and structure. But it does not melt completely.
87166.m: Metamorphic rocks form by being changed under pressure and heat.

87167.q: What does the Greek word metamorphosis mean?
87167.e: Metamorphosis means transformation or change of form. The word is also used for a caterpillar changing into a butterfly.

87168.q: Which metamorphic rock forms from sandstone?
87168.e: Sandstone is made mainly of grains of quartz. Under pressure and heat, they grow together into a very hard rock, quartzite.

87169.q: What happens if a rock deep down is not just changed but melts completely?
87169.e: Metamorphism only takes place in the solid state. If the rock melts completely, magma forms, which later becomes an igneous rock.
87169.m: If a rock melts completely, it becomes magma.

87170.q: Where do metamorphic rocks form in large amounts?
a: Deep inside mountains as they are built
At the bottom of shallow lakes
87170.e: When continental plates collide, rocks are pushed deep down and strongly squeezed. This regional metamorphism also shaped many rocks of the Alps.
87170.m: Large amounts of metamorphic rock form when mountains are built.

87171.q: What is the change of rock that lies right next to hot magma called?
87171.e: When magma pushes into the Earth’s crust, the rock next to it is strongly heated. Where it touches the molten rock, it is changed.
87171.m: Contact metamorphism is caused by the heat of nearby magma.

87172.q: Why are the minerals in many metamorphic rocks lined up in parallel?
a: Because of pressure from one particular direction
Because of gravity as they fall
Because of wind at the surface
Because of the current in rivers
87172.e: When a rock is strongly squeezed from one side, flat minerals line up across the pressure. This makes the rock look striped or layered.
87172.m: Pressure from one direction lines up the minerals in metamorphic rocks.

87173.q: Why did people in Ticino and the Grisons build stoves from the soft stone called lavez?
87173.e: Lavez, also called soapstone or pot stone, is soft and stores heat very well. Cooking pots used to be turned from it, and stoves are still built from it today.
87173.m: Lavez is a soft stone that stores heat well.

87174.q: Which of the following groups of rocks can be changed by metamorphism?
87174.e: Igneous, sedimentary and even metamorphic rocks can be changed again. What matters is that pressure and temperature change a lot.
87174.m: Any kind of rock can be changed by metamorphism.

87175.q: What does the rock cycle describe?
a: How rocks change into one another over a long time
How stones roll in a stream
How crystals grow in a laboratory
87175.e: Rocks are worn away, deposited, buried, changed, melted and lifted again. So the same material becomes new rocks again and again.
87175.m: In the rock cycle, rocks change again and again.

87176.q: What are the three main groups of rocks in the rock cycle?
87176.e: Rocks are grouped by how they formed. Solidified molten rock, hardened deposits and changed rocks make up the three groups.
87176.m: There are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

87177.q: Which rock forms when sand is deposited on the seabed and hardens over a long time?
87177.e: Layer by layer, the sand is pressed together and cemented. This forms a sedimentary rock, sandstone.

87178.q: Which two sources of energy drive the rock cycle?
a: The heat inside the Earth and energy from the Sun
87178.e: The Earth’s heat melts and moves rock deep down. The Sun drives the weather and the water cycle, and with them weathering and erosion at the surface.
87178.m: The Earth’s heat and the Sun’s energy keep the rock cycle going.

87179.q: Roughly how long does it take for a rock to go once through the cycle?
87179.e: Erosion, deposition, burial and uplift happen extremely slowly. A full round usually takes many millions to hundreds of millions of years.
87179.m: One round of the rock cycle takes millions of years.

87180.q: Where is rock from the Earth’s crust pushed back into the mantle in large amounts?
a: At the bottom of mountain lakes
87180.e: At subduction zones, one tectonic plate sinks beneath another. Rock goes down to great depths, where it is changed or melted.
87180.m: At subduction zones, rock sinks into the Earth’s mantle.

87181.q: How do rocks that were changed deep in the Earth get back to the surface?
a: Through uplift and erosion of the layers above
87181.e: When mountains are built, blocks of rock are lifted up. At the same time, water and ice wear away the upper layers until the deep rocks become visible.
87181.m: Uplift and erosion bring deep rocks to the surface.

87182.q: In the rock cycle, what happens to a sedimentary rock that is buried deep and strongly heated?
87182.e: With increasing depth, pressure and temperature rise. The sedimentary rock is changed; for example, limestone becomes marble.
87182.m: Buried sedimentary rocks become metamorphic rocks.

87183.q: What happens to a rock at the Earth’s surface that is exposed to wind, water and frost?
a: It is slowly broken up and worn away
87183.e: At the surface, weather and water attack every rock. The fragments are carried away and later deposited as sediment.
87183.m: At the surface, every rock is slowly broken up and worn away.

87184.e: Basalt contains many dark minerals that are rich in iron and magnesium. That is why it is dark grey to black.
87184.m: Basalt is a dark, almost black rock.

87185.q: What is the floor of the oceans mostly made of?
87185.e: At the mid-ocean ridges, basalt lava constantly comes out. It forms the oceanic crust, which makes up most of the seabed.
87185.m: The seabed is mostly made of basalt.

87186.q: What shape do thick basalt flows often take as they cool slowly?
87186.e: As it cools, the lava shrinks and cracks. The cracks often form a pattern of mostly six-sided columns.
87186.m: Cooling basalt often breaks into six-sided columns.

87187.q: Where is the famous Giant’s Causeway with about 40,000 basalt columns?
87187.e: The Giant’s Causeway lies on the north coast of Northern Ireland. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
87187.m: The Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland is made of basalt columns.

87188.q: Which island in the North Atlantic is made mostly of basalt?
87188.e: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and on a hotspot. The many volcanic eruptions built the island out of basalt lava.
87188.m: Iceland is an island made of basalt.

87189.q: How does the lava of basalt volcanoes such as those on Hawaii usually behave?
a: It is runny and flows in long streams
It stays as a solid plug in the crater
It only flies into the air as ash
It is cold and does not flow at all
87189.e: Basalt lava is very hot and contains few substances that make it thick. So it flows easily and forms long lava flows.

87190.q: What are the dark areas on the Moon called lunar seas really?
87190.e: More than three billion years ago, runny lava filled huge impact basins on the Moon. The dark basalt stands out clearly from the lighter highlands.
87190.m: The lunar seas are plains of dark basalt.

87191.q: Which insulation material for houses is made from melted basalt and similar rock?
87191.e: Basalt is melted at a very high temperature and blown into fine fibres. This makes rock wool, which protects houses from cold and fire.
87191.m: Basalt can be used to make rock wool for insulation.

87192.q: How can you usually recognise gneiss?
a: By its light and dark stripes
87192.e: In gneiss, light minerals such as quartz and feldspar and dark ones such as mica are arranged in layers. This gives it a striped look.
87192.m: You can recognise gneiss by its light and dark stripes.

87193.q: What does granite become when it is strongly squeezed and heated deep in the Earth?
87193.e: Under high pressure and high temperature, the minerals of granite line up in layers. This turns it into gneiss.

87194.q: Where did the gneiss in the upper part of the Matterhorn originally come from?
87194.e: The summit pyramid of the Matterhorn is made of gneiss from the Dent Blanche nappe. This rock was once part of a piece of Africa that was pushed over European rock when the Alps formed.
87194.m: The gneiss at the top of the Matterhorn originally came from the African Plate.

87195.q: What is so-called “Ticino granite” usually, from a geological point of view?
87195.e: The building stones quarried in Ticino are often sold as granite. But geologically they are gneisses, taken from the quarries in Ticino’s valleys.

87196.q: What are the traditional roofs of many stone houses in Ticino covered with?
87196.e: Gneiss can be split along its layers into thick slabs. These heavy stone slabs cover the roofs of many rustici in Ticino.
87196.m: Many rustici in Ticino have roofs made of gneiss slabs.

87197.q: Which rocks does the Acasta gneiss in Canada belong to?
a: The oldest known rocks on Earth
87197.e: The Acasta gneiss in north-western Canada is about 4 billion years old. That makes it one of the oldest known rocks on Earth.
87197.m: The Acasta gneiss is one of the oldest rocks on Earth.

87198.q: What are the “eyes” in augen gneiss?
a: Drops of water in the stone
87198.e: In some gneisses, single feldspar crystals have been shaped into oval lenses. The stripes flow around them, so they look like eyes.
87198.m: The eyes in augen gneiss are oval feldspar crystals.

87199.q: Does gneiss form at a lower or higher temperature than slate?
87199.e: Slate forms through weak metamorphism. Gneiss only forms through strong metamorphism, often at temperatures of several hundred degrees deep in the Earth’s crust.
87199.m: Gneiss forms through strong metamorphism at high temperature.

87200.q: In which part of Switzerland do you find especially a lot of gneiss?
87200.e: In the Central Alps, for example around the Gotthard or in Ticino, deeply buried rocks have come to the surface through uplift. Many of them are gneisses.
87200.m: Gneiss is widespread in the Swiss Central Alps.

87201.q: Which property is typical of slate?
a: It can be split into thin slabs
87201.e: The minerals in slate are lined up in parallel. Along these surfaces the rock can be split into thin, smooth slabs.
87201.m: Slate can be split into thin slabs.

87202.q: Which rock does slate form from?
87202.e: When claystone is squeezed deep down and slightly heated, slate forms. It is one of the weakly changed rocks.

87203.q: What did schoolchildren often write on in the past, before exercise books became cheap?
87203.e: Slates were smooth, dark and could be wiped clean again and again. Many came from slate mines, including some in Switzerland.
87203.m: Schoolchildren used to write on slates.

87204.q: What did people use to write on a slate in the past?
87204.e: The slate pencil was a thin stick, often made of soft slate itself. It left pale lines on the slate.
87204.m: You wrote on a slate with a slate pencil.

87205.q: What was slate from the Glarus region mainly used for in the past?
a: For writing slates, tables and roofs
87205.e: At the Landesplattenberg near Engi, slate was mined for centuries for writing slates, tables and roofs. Today you can visit the mine.
87205.m: Slate was mined in the Glarus region for a long time.

87206.q: Which fossils are especially well known in Glarus slate?
87206.e: Glarus slate formed from fine mud in a sea. Fish were preserved especially well in it.
87206.m: Fossil fish are found in Glarus slate.

87207.q: Bündner schist shapes many mountains in the Grisons. What did it originally form from?
a: From the deposits of an ancient sea
From the lava of a volcano
From the sand dunes of a desert
87207.e: Bündner schist formed from the deposits of an ancient sea and was changed when the Alps were formed. It makes up large parts of the mountains of the Grisons.
87207.m: Bündner schist formed from the deposits of an ancient sea.

87208.q: Why does mica schist glitter in the light?
a: It contains lots of tiny mica flakes
87208.e: Mica schist has been changed more strongly than slate. The mica flakes that grew in it reflect the light and make it glitter.
87208.m: Mica schist glitters because of its mica flakes.

87209.q: Which type of rock does Nagelfluh belong to?
87209.e: A conglomerate is made of rounded stones cemented together by a binding material. Nagelfluh is such a sedimentary rock.
87209.m: Nagelfluh is a conglomerate made of rounded stones.

87210.q: Where does Nagelfluh get its name from?
a: The stones look like nail heads in a rock face
It was used for making nails
It is as hard as iron nails
It was discovered by a Mr Nagel
87210.e: When the pebbles stick out of the rock face, they look like the heads of nails. In German, Nagel means nail, and Fluh is a Swiss word for rock.
87210.m: Nagelfluh means rock with stones like nail heads.

87211.q: Why are the stones in Nagelfluh round?
a: They were carried a long way by rivers
They are made of drops of lava
87211.e: While being carried by rivers, the stones knock against each other and lose their edges. So they became round pebbles before they were deposited.
87211.m: The stones in Nagelfluh were ground round in rivers.

87212.q: Where do the pebbles of Swiss Nagelfluh come from?
a: From the Alps, which were forming at the time
From the seabed of the Atlantic
87212.e: While the Alps were being lifted up, rivers carried huge amounts of debris into the land in front of them. There they deposited it in large fans of debris.
87212.m: The pebbles of Nagelfluh come from the young Alps.

87213.q: Which mountain on the border between the cantons of Bern and Lucerne is made of Nagelfluh?
87213.e: The Napf is a large former fan of debris made of Nagelfluh. Its deeply cut ravines are typical of this rock.
87213.m: The Napf is a mountain made of Nagelfluh.

87214.q: In which landslide in the canton of Schwyz did layers of Nagelfluh slide off the Rossberg in 1806?
87214.e: On 2 September 1806, layers of Nagelfluh slid off the Rossberg on softened marl. The landslide destroyed Goldau and killed around 450 people.
87214.m: In the Goldau landslide of 1806, Nagelfluh slid off the Rossberg.

87215.q: Because of its look, what do Swiss people jokingly call Nagelfluh?
87215.e: Nagelfluh looks like concrete with gravel in it. That is why it is jokingly called the Lord’s concrete, meaning concrete made by nature.
87215.m: Nagelfluh is also called the Lord’s concrete.

87216.q: What holds the pebbles in Nagelfluh together?
a: A natural binding material made of lime and sand
87216.e: Fine sand and lime were deposited between the pebbles. Over time this mass became hard and cemented the stones together.
87216.m: Lime and sand cement the stones of Nagelfluh together.

87217.q: What does molasse mean in geology?
a: Debris worn away from the Alps, lying in front of them
Glacier ice in the Central Plateau
87217.e: As the Alps were lifted up, a lot of rock was worn away. This debris filled the basin north of the Alps and became rock: the molasse.
87217.m: The molasse is made of debris worn away from the Alps.

87218.q: In which large region of Switzerland does the molasse form the ground underneath?
87218.e: The Central Plateau lies in the molasse basin between the Alps and the Jura. Under the Ice Age deposits there is molasse almost everywhere.
87218.m: The Swiss Central Plateau lies on molasse.

87219.q: Which rocks are mainly found in the molasse?
87219.e: Depending on the current, rivers deposited coarse pebbles, sand or fine mud. These became Nagelfluh, sandstone and marl.
87219.m: Sandstone, marl and Nagelfluh are found in the molasse.

87220.q: Which rock are many houses in Bern’s old town built from?
87220.e: After the great fire of 1405, Bern was rebuilt with sandstone from the surrounding area. This Bern sandstone formed from Alpine debris in a shallow sea.
87220.m: Bern’s old town is built from molasse sandstone.

87221.q: Roughly when was the molasse deposited?
87221.e: The molasse formed while the Alps were being folded up. Deposition began about 34 million years ago and ended about 5 million years ago.
87221.m: The molasse formed about 35 to 5 million years ago.

87222.q: What covered the area of today’s Central Plateau for a while about 20 million years ago?
87222.e: About 20 million years ago, the sea flowed into the basin north of the Alps. That is why shells and even sharks’ teeth are found in these layers.
87222.m: About 20 million years ago, there was a sea in the Central Plateau.

87223.q: Which mountain on the edge of the Alps is made of tilted layers of molasse?
87223.e: On the northern edge of the Alps, the molasse layers were pushed together and tilted when the mountains formed. The Rigi is made of such layers of Nagelfluh.
87223.m: The Rigi is made of tilted molasse.

87224.q: How far does the molasse basin north of the Alps stretch?
a: Only from Lake Constance to Zurich
87224.e: The molasse basin runs as a long trough, about 1000 kilometres long, along the northern edge of the Alps. It begins in the west at Lake Geneva and reaches through southern Germany to Austria.
87224.m: The molasse basin stretches from Lake Geneva to Austria.

a: Rock breaking down where it is
87225.e: In weathering, rock is loosened and broken down by weather, water and living things. At first it stays in the same place.
87225.m: Weathering is rock breaking down where it is.

87226.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
a: Weathering breaks rock up, erosion carries it away
Weathering only happens in the sea
87226.e: Weathering prepares the rock by loosening it. Only in erosion do water, ice or wind carry the particles away.
87226.m: Weathering loosens rock, erosion carries it away.

87227.q: What kind of weathering is it when rainwater slowly dissolves limestone?
87227.e: Rainwater contains a little carbonic acid, which can dissolve lime. Because the substances change in the process, it is called chemical weathering.
87227.m: Rainwater dissolving lime is chemical weathering.

87228.q: What is it called when plant roots push rocks apart?
87228.e: Roots grow into fine cracks and get thicker. With great force they widen the cracks until the rock breaks. This is a type of biological weathering.
87228.m: In root wedging, plant roots break rock apart.

87229.q: Why do rocks in deserts often break apart through temperature weathering?
a: Because of big differences between day and night
87229.e: In deserts, rock gets very hot during the day and cools down a lot at night. Constant expanding and shrinking causes cracks.
87229.m: Strong temperature changes make rock break apart in deserts.

87230.q: In salt weathering, what breaks the rock apart?
a: Salt crystals growing in the pores
87230.e: Salty water gets into the pores and evaporates. The growing salt crystals push the rock apart, especially on coasts and in dry areas.
87230.m: Growing salt crystals can break rock apart.

87231.q: In which climate is chemical weathering strongest?
a: In the hot, humid climate of the tropics
In the cold climate of the polar regions
In the dry climate of deserts
In high mountains above the snow line
87231.e: Chemical processes happen faster in warmth and need water. That is why rock breaks down especially deeply in the hot, humid tropics.
87231.m: Chemical weathering is strongest in the tropics.

87232.q: Over a long time, what does rainwater carve out of bare limestone rocks such as those on the Schrattenfluh?
87232.e: Rainwater contains a little carbonic acid and slowly dissolves the lime. This creates grooves that can be up to a metre deep. They are called karren.
87232.m: Rainwater carves grooves into limestone rocks.

87233.e: When water, wind or ice can no longer carry material, it settles. This process is called sedimentation.
87233.m: Sedimentation is the depositing of particles.

87234.q: When does a river deposit especially a lot of material?
87234.e: Fast water can carry a lot of material. When the current slows down, for example where it flows into a lake, the particles sink to the bottom.

87235.q: Which particles settle first in a river that is slowing down?
a: All of them at the same time
87235.e: Large stones and gravel sink first, because the water can only carry them with a lot of force. Fine sand and clay are carried further.
87235.m: Coarse particles settle first, fine ones later.

87236.q: What is the landform called that forms when a river deposits a lot of material at its mouth?
87236.e: At its mouth, the river loses its force and deposits material. Land grows out into the lake or sea, like the Maggia delta near Locarno.
87236.m: A delta forms from deposits at a river mouth.

87237.q: Why is a large delta growing where the Kander flows into Lake Thun?
a: The Kander deposits a lot of gravel and sand there
A glacier pushes debris into the lake there
The wind blows sand in there
87237.e: Since 1714, the Kander has flowed into Lake Thun through a man-made cut. In the calm lake water it deposits so much material that a large delta has formed.
87237.m: Since 1714, the Kander has been building a delta into Lake Thun.

87238.q: In undisturbed deposits, which layer is normally the oldest?
