90178.q: Where are the products of an endothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
90178.e: The products have stored the energy that was taken in. That is why they are higher than the starting materials.
90178.m: In endothermic reactions the products have more energy than the starting materials.

90179.q: Why must the kiln be heated strongly the whole time when making quicklime?
a: Lime gives off a lot of heat
90179.e: Limestone only breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide at around 900 °C. The reaction keeps taking in heat and stops without heating.
90179.m: Making quicklime needs a constant supply of heat.

90180.q: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. What happens if you switch the electricity off?
90180.e: The electrolysis of water is endothermic. It needs a constant supply of electrical energy and stops at once without electricity.
90180.m: Endothermic reactions only run with a constant supply of energy.

90181.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘endo’ in the word endothermic mean?
90181.e: ‘Endo’ means ‘inside’ or ‘in’. In an endothermic reaction, heat goes into the system.
90181.m: Endothermic means that heat goes in.

90182.q: What is meant by activation energy?
a: The energy a reaction needs to start
The energy released at the end
90182.e: For particles to react, bonds must first be loosened. The starting energy needed for this is called activation energy.
90182.m: Activation energy gets a reaction going.

90183.q: Where does the activation energy come from when you strike a match?
a: From the moisture in the air
From the light in the room
From the weight of the match
90183.e: Rubbing the match on the striking surface creates heat. This heat starts the reaction in the match head.
90183.m: The heat of friction can start a reaction.

90184.q: Why does a piece of wood on the table not burn by itself, even though oxygen is there?
90184.e: Burning wood does release energy, but it must be started first. At room temperature there is not enough energy for this.
90184.m: Without starting energy, even burning does not begin.

90185.q: How is activation energy shown in an energy diagram?
a: As an energy hill before the products
As a valley below the starting materials
As an arrow pointing down at the end
90185.e: From the starting materials the curve first rises before it leads to the products. The height of this hill is the activation energy.
90185.m: The activation energy is the energy hill a reaction must get over.

90186.q: What provides the activation energy for combustion in a petrol engine?
a: The spark from the spark plug
90186.e: The spark plug makes an electric spark. It ignites the mixture of petrol vapour and air in the cylinder.
90186.m: In a petrol engine, a spark starts the combustion.

90187.q: Why do many reactions happen faster at higher temperatures?
a: More particles have enough energy to start
90187.e: The warmer it is, the faster the particles move. So more collisions reach the necessary activation energy.
90187.m: Heat helps to reach the activation energy.

90188.q: When does a collision between two particles lead to a reaction?
a: When the particles are the same size
When the particles are standing still
90188.e: Only collisions with at least the activation energy are successful. Weaker collisions make the particles bounce apart unchanged.
90188.m: Only collisions with enough energy lead to a reaction.

90189.q: What does a catalyst do to the energy hill of a reaction?
90189.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy. This makes the reaction start more easily and run faster.
90189.m: A catalyst lowers the energy hill.

90190.q: What does a catalyst do in a chemical reaction?
a: It speeds it up without being used up
It increases the mass of the products
90190.e: A catalyst makes a reaction run faster. At the end it is still there, unchanged.
90190.m: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up itself.

90191.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
90191.e: The catalyst makes a different reaction path possible, with a smaller energy hill. So more particles react in the same time.
90191.m: A catalyst makes the energy hill smaller.

90192.q: Which poisonous gas does a car's catalytic converter turn into carbon dioxide?
90192.e: Carbon monoxide is very poisonous. In the catalytic converter it reacts with oxygen to form less dangerous carbon dioxide.
90192.m: The catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

90193.q: Which precious metal works in many catalytic converters?
90193.e: Catalytic converters contain thin layers of platinum, palladium or rhodium. These metals speed up the conversion of the exhaust gases.
90193.m: Platinum is an important metal in the catalytic converter.

90194.q: What are the catalysts in living things called?
90194.e: Enzymes are mostly proteins that speed up reactions in the body. Without them, digestion, for example, would be far too slow.
90194.m: Enzymes are the catalysts of living things.

90195.q: Why does bread taste slightly sweet after you chew it for a long time?
a: An enzyme in saliva splits starch into sugar
The bread gets warm in the mouth
90195.e: Saliva contains an enzyme that splits starch into smaller sugar particles. That is why bread tastes sweetish after long chewing.
90195.m: An enzyme in saliva breaks starch down into sugar.

90196.q: Why does industry use catalysts in many manufacturing processes?
a: The reactions run faster and need less energy
The catalyst becomes the finished product
90196.e: Catalysts speed up reactions, often at lower temperatures too. This saves time, energy and money.
90196.m: Catalysts save time and energy in industry.

90197.q: If you add manganese dioxide to hydrogen peroxide, it foams a lot. Which gas forms?
90197.e: Manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst and speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. This produces water and oxygen.
90197.m: Manganese dioxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

90198.q: Where is the catalytic converter in a car?
90198.e: The catalytic converter is built into the exhaust pipe. The exhaust gases flow through it and are turned into less harmful substances.
90198.m: The catalytic converter cleans the exhaust gases in the exhaust.

90199.q: Why does food go off more slowly in the fridge?
a: There is no air at all in the fridge
The light in the fridge kills germs
90199.e: At low temperatures the particles move more slowly. So breakdown and decay happen more slowly.

90200.q: What usually happens to a chemical reaction when you raise the temperature?
90200.e: At higher temperatures the particles move faster and collide more often. That is why most reactions run faster.

90201.q: Why do wood shavings burn faster than a whole log?
a: They have a larger surface area
90201.e: The more finely a substance is divided, the more particles are at the surface. That is where the oxygen can attack.

90202.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. In which acid is it faster?
90202.e: Concentrated acid has more acid particles per volume. So there are more collisions with the metal.
90202.m: A higher concentration speeds up a reaction.

90203.q: What does the rate of reaction tell you?
a: How much the amount of a substance changes per unit of time
90203.e: You measure how much starting material disappears or how much product forms per unit of time. This gives the rate of reaction.
90203.m: The rate of reaction describes the change per unit of time.

90204.q: Why can fine flour dust in the air explode?
a: The huge surface area reacts in a flash
90204.e: Every tiny grain of flour is surrounded by air. A spark can therefore set off an extremely fast combustion, a dust explosion.
90204.m: Fine dust in the air can burn explosively.

90205.q: Why do reactions run faster at higher temperatures?
a: The particles collide more often and harder
90205.e: Warmer particles move faster. There are more collisions, and more of them have enough energy for a reaction.
90205.m: Heat makes particles faster and reactions more frequent.

90206.q: Marble reacts with hydrochloric acid and forms a gas. How can you measure the rate of reaction?
a: Measure the amount of gas produced per minute
Look at the colour of the acid
Measure the length of the glass
90206.e: You collect the gas and read off the volume at fixed time intervals. The more gas per minute, the faster the reaction.
90206.m: The amount of gas per unit of time shows how fast a reaction is.

90207.q: When 10 g of limestone is heated, 5.6 g of quicklime and a gas are produced. How much gas escapes?
90207.e: The total mass stays the same, so the escaping carbon dioxide weighs 10 g minus 5.6 g = 4.4 g.
90207.m: You can work out the mass of an escaping gas from the difference in mass.

90208.q: Matches burn in a sealed jar on a scale. What does the scale show afterwards?
90208.e: In the sealed jar, no gas can escape and none can get in. That is why the mass stays the same.
90208.m: In a sealed container the mass does not change during a reaction.

90209.q: Steel wool is burnt on a scale and is heavier afterwards. Why?
a: The iron has combined with oxygen from the air
90209.e: When it burns, iron combines with oxygen to form iron oxide. The mass of the oxygen is added.
90209.m: When a substance combines with oxygen, it gets heavier.

90210.q: Two substances react completely to form 50 g of product. One of the substances weighed 30 g. How heavy was the other?
90210.e: Both starting materials together must weigh 50 g. So 50 g minus 30 g = 20 g.
90210.m: You can work out the mass of a missing starting material from the mass of the product.

90211.q: 56 g of iron reacts completely with 32 g of sulphur. How much iron sulphide forms?
90211.e: According to the law of conservation of mass: 56 g + 32 g = 88 g of iron sulphide.
90211.m: Add up the masses of the starting materials to get the mass of the product.

90212.q: 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen. How much carbon dioxide forms?
90212.e: The masses of the starting materials together give the mass of the product: 12 g + 32 g = 44 g.
90212.m: Mass is also conserved when carbon burns.

90213.q: A candle gets lighter as it burns. Where does the mass go?
a: Into gases that escape into the air
90213.e: The wax reacts to form carbon dioxide and water vapour. These gases spread into the air, which is why the scale shows less.
90213.m: When gases escape, a substance seems to get lighter.

90214.q: What must be the same on both sides of a correct chemical equation?
a: The number of each kind of atom
90214.e: In reactions, atoms are only joined up in new ways, not created or destroyed. That is why each kind of atom must appear equally often on the left and right.
90214.m: In a chemical equation, the number of each kind of atom matches on the left and right.

90215.q: Which country did the chemist Antoine de Lavoisier come from?
90215.e: Lavoisier was born in Paris in 1743. He is one of the best-known French scientists.
90215.m: Antoine de Lavoisier was a French chemist.

90216.q: Which old theory about burning did Lavoisier disprove?
90216.e: According to the phlogiston theory, a substance called phlogiston was supposed to escape during burning. Lavoisier showed that burning substances instead combine with a part of the air.
90216.m: Lavoisier explained burning as a reaction with oxygen.

90217.q: What French name did Lavoisier give to oxygen?
90217.e: ‘Oxygène’ means ‘acid former’, because Lavoisier believed the substance was found in all acids. This is also where the chemical symbol O comes from.

90218.q: How did Antoine de Lavoisier die in 1794?
90218.e: Lavoisier collected taxes for the king. During the French Revolution a court sentenced him for this, and he died on the guillotine in Paris.
90218.m: Lavoisier lost his life in the French Revolution.

90219.q: Which measuring instrument was especially important for Lavoisier's experiments?
90219.e: Lavoisier weighed substances very precisely before and after a reaction. In this way he realised that the total mass stays the same.
90219.m: Lavoisier made the precise balance the most important tool in chemistry.

90220.q: As Lavoisier showed, which gas from the air do burning substances combine with?
90220.e: Lavoisier realised that part of the air is used up during burning. He called this substance oxygen.
90220.m: When substances burn, they combine with oxygen.

90221.q: Lavoisier's famous textbook came out in 1789. Which event began in the same year?
a: The founding of the Swiss Confederation
90221.e: The textbook ‘Traité élémentaire de chimie’ came out in 1789. In the same year, citizens in Paris stormed the Bastille.
90221.m: Lavoisier's textbook came out in the year of the French Revolution.

90222.q: What did Lavoisier show about water?
a: It is a compound of two elements
It is an element that cannot be split
90222.e: For a long time water was thought to be a basic element. Lavoisier showed that it can be split and also built up from hydrogen and oxygen.
90222.m: Water is not an element but a compound.

90223.q: Because of his work, what is Antoine de Lavoisier often called?
90223.e: With precise measurements, clear names for substances and the law of conservation of mass, he laid the foundations of today's chemistry.
90223.m: Lavoisier is seen as the founder of modern chemistry.

90224.q: Why are balloons filled with helium today instead of hydrogen?
90224.e: Hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. Helium is also lighter than air, but it does not burn.
90224.m: Mixed with air, hydrogen catches fire very easily.

90225.q: How do you hold the test tube for the hydrogen pop test?
90225.e: Hydrogen is much lighter than air and would escape upwards out of an open, upright tube. That is why you hold the opening downwards.
90225.m: Because hydrogen is so light, you hold the tube upside down.

90226.q: How can you tell that the hydrogen pop test is positive?
a: By a whistling or squeaky pop sound
90226.e: The gas burns very quickly in the tube. This makes a typical whistle or a short pop.
90226.m: A whistle or pop in the pop test shows hydrogen.

a: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen
A mixture of nitrogen and argon
90227.e: Oxyhydrogen is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Even a small spark makes it react violently.
90227.m: Oxyhydrogen is an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.

90228.q: Which substance forms when oxyhydrogen reacts?
90228.e: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. After the test you can sometimes see tiny droplets in the tube.

90229.q: In what ratio by volume do hydrogen and oxygen in oxyhydrogen react most violently?
90229.e: A water molecule needs two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. That is why a mixture of two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen reacts most violently.
90229.m: In oxyhydrogen there are two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen.

90230.q: What do you hear when there is almost pure hydrogen in the test tube?
90230.e: Pure hydrogen burns quietly at the opening, because there is hardly any oxygen in the tube. It only whistles loudly when air is mixed in.
90230.m: Pure hydrogen burns with a quiet sound.

90231.q: Which reaction is often used in the school lab to make hydrogen for the pop test?
90231.e: Base metals such as zinc react with hydrochloric acid. Bubbles of hydrogen rise up.
90231.m: Zinc and hydrochloric acid produce hydrogen in the lab.

90232.q: Why must the valves of oxygen cylinders never be lubricated with oil or grease?
a: Oil can catch fire violently in pure oxygen
Oil blocks the cylinder at once
90232.e: In pure oxygen, substances burn much more violently than in air. Oil and grease can even catch fire by themselves there.
90232.m: Pure oxygen and oil are a dangerous mix.

90233.q: What do you see in a positive glowing splint test?
a: The glowing splint bursts into a bright flame
90233.e: In pure oxygen, wood burns much more strongly than in air. That is why the glowing tip relights with a bright flame.
90233.m: A glowing splint that relights shows oxygen.

a: A wooden splint that glows but does not burn
A metal rod with a battery
A small glass tube with gas
90234.e: You light a wooden splint and blow out the flame. What remains is a glowing tip that only smoulders.
90234.m: A glowing splint is a glowing piece of wood without a flame.

90235.q: Why does a glowing splint not relight in normal air?
a: Air contains only about 21 per cent oxygen
90235.e: To relight, the splint needs much more oxygen than there is in normal air. There it just keeps glowing.
90235.m: Normal air has too little oxygen to relight a glowing splint.

90236.q: What happens to a glowing splint in carbon dioxide?
a: It bursts into a bright flame
90236.e: Carbon dioxide does not support burning. The glowing wood lacks oxygen and goes out.
90236.m: A glowing splint goes out in carbon dioxide.

90237.q: What are substances such as oxygen called that strongly help things burn?
90237.e: Oxygen does not burn itself, but it makes burning much more violent. Such substances are called oxidising.
90237.m: Oxygen is not flammable, but it is oxidising.

90238.q: Which hazard symbol is on cylinders of pure oxygen?
90238.e: The symbol with a flame over a circle marks oxidising substances. It warns that fires can become much more violent.
90238.m: A flame over a circle warns of oxidising substances.

90239.q: In the light, water plants form gas bubbles that relight a glowing splint. Which process makes the gas?
90239.e: Photosynthesis produces oxygen as well as glucose. The plant releases it into the water as bubbles.
90239.m: Plants give off oxygen during photosynthesis.

90240.q: Which gas is detected with the limewater test?
90240.e: You bubble the gas through limewater. If it turns cloudy, that shows carbon dioxide.
90240.m: The limewater test detects carbon dioxide.

90241.q: What do you see in a positive limewater test?
a: The limewater turns milky and cloudy
90241.e: Fine white particles form in the clear limewater. This makes the liquid look milky.
90241.m: If limewater turns cloudy, carbon dioxide is present.

a: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
90242.e: Limewater is made by dissolving slaked lime, that is calcium hydroxide, in water and filtering it. It is clear and colourless.
90242.m: Limewater is clear, dissolved calcium hydroxide.

90243.q: Which substance makes limewater go cloudy in the limewater test?
90243.e: Carbon dioxide reacts with the dissolved calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate. This chalk hardly dissolves and appears as a white cloudiness.
90243.m: In the limewater test, calcium carbonate forms.

90244.q: Roughly how much carbon dioxide does the air you breathe out contain?
90244.e: Air you breathe in contains only about 0.04 per cent carbon dioxide; air you breathe out contains about a hundred times more. That is why limewater goes cloudy quickly when you blow into it through a straw.
90244.m: Breathed-out air contains much more carbon dioxide than breathed-in air.

90245.q: The gases from a candle flame turn limewater cloudy. What does this tell you about the candle wax?
90245.e: The carbon dioxide detected can only form if the fuel contains carbon. The oxygen comes from the air.
90245.m: Carbon dioxide from a flame shows there is carbon in the fuel.

90246.q: Why does limewater go cloudy when you blow into it through a straw?
90246.e: Breathed-out air contains a lot of carbon dioxide. It reacts with the limewater, white chalk forms and the water turns milky.
90246.m: Breathed-out air turns limewater cloudy because it contains carbon dioxide.

90247.q: Is limewater acidic, neutral or alkaline?
90247.e: Calcium hydroxide is a base. Limewater has a pH of about 12 and turns universal indicator blue to violet.

90248.q: When lighting a fire, why does it help to blow gently on the embers?
a: The wind removes the ash as fuel
90248.e: Blowing pushes fresh air onto the glowing parts. With more oxygen, the fire burns more strongly.
90248.m: More oxygen makes a fire burn more strongly.

90249.q: What happens if one side of the fire triangle is missing?
90249.e: All three conditions must be met at the same time. If you remove one of them, burning cannot continue.
90249.m: If one side of the triangle is missing, the fire goes out.

90250.q: Someone pours sand onto a campfire. Which side of the triangle does this remove?
90250.e: The sand covers the embers. No fresh air can reach the fuel any more.
90250.m: Covering a fire smothers it because oxygen is missing.

90251.q: Water is sprayed onto a wood fire. Which condition does this mainly remove?
90251.e: Water takes in a great deal of heat as it warms up and evaporates. The wood cools below its ignition temperature.
90251.m: Water puts out a fire by cooling it.

90252.q: During a forest fire, firefighters cut down trees to make a firebreak. What are they taking away from the fire?
90252.e: In the firebreak there is nothing left that could burn. The fire cannot spread any further there.
90252.m: Without fuel, a fire cannot spread.

90253.q: What is the ignition temperature of a substance?
a: The lowest temperature at which it catches fire by itself
The temperature at which it melts
The temperature at which it freezes
90253.e: Only from its ignition temperature upwards does a substance start burning in air by itself. Every substance has its own ignition temperature.
90253.m: Below its ignition temperature, a substance does not catch fire by itself.

90254.q: You turn off the gas tap on a gas cooker. Why does the flame go out?
90254.e: Without gas flowing in, there is nothing left to burn. The flame goes out at once.
90254.m: Stopping the fuel supply puts out the fire.

90255.q: Why does a candle under an upside-down glass go out after a short time?
a: The oxygen in the glass gets used up
90255.e: The flame uses up the oxygen under the glass. No new air can flow in, so it goes out.
90255.m: A flame constantly needs fresh oxygen.

90256.q: Why must you never put out burning oil in a pan with water?
a: The water turns to steam instantly and throws burning oil out
The water makes the oil colder
The water turns the oil black
The water dissolves the oil at once
90256.e: Water sinks beneath the hot oil and turns to steam explosively. Burning oil sprays everywhere. Instead, you cover the pan with a lid or a fire blanket.
90256.m: Never put out a fat fire with water; cover it instead.

90257.q: Which materials belong to fire class A?
a: Solid materials that form embers, such as wood and paper
90257.e: Fire class A covers solid materials that burn with embers. These include wood, paper, textiles and coal.
90257.m: Wood and paper belong to fire class A.

90258.q: Which fire extinguisher is suitable for computer rooms because it leaves no residue?
90258.e: Carbon dioxide pushes away the oxygen and then evaporates completely. Electrical equipment is not left dirty.
90258.m: A carbon dioxide extinguisher puts out fires cleanly without residue.

90259.q: How does a foam extinguisher put out burning petrol?
a: The foam forms a blanket over the liquid
The foam turns petrol into water
The foam makes the petrol heavier
90259.e: The foam floats on the burning liquid. It separates it from the air and cools it at the same time.
90259.m: A blanket of foam separates burning liquids from the air.

90260.q: Which fire extinguisher works on fire classes A, B and C but leaves a lot of dust?
90260.e: The extinguishing powder works on solids, liquids and gases. Afterwards, though, fine dust lies everywhere and can damage equipment.
90260.m: An ABC powder extinguisher is versatile but makes a lot of mess.

90262.q: What is the best way to put out burning magnesium?
a: With dry sand or metal fire powder
90262.e: Burning metals react violently with water and even with carbon dioxide. Dry sand or special powder smothers the fire safely.
90262.m: Metal fires are put out with dry sand or special powder.

90263.q: Which fire class stands for flammable liquids such as petrol and alcohol?
90263.e: Fire class B covers liquids and substances that become liquid when they burn, such as petrol, alcohol or wax.
90263.m: Burning liquids belong to fire class B.

a: A description of an algorithm in simple, semi-formal language
A real programming language for robots
90459.e: Pseudocode describes the steps of an algorithm in a similar way to a program, but without the strict rules of a programming language. It is meant for people.
90459.m: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in simple, program-like language.

90460.q: Can a computer run pseudocode directly?
a: No, it first has to be translated into a programming language
Yes, but only on a mobile phone
No, it is only printed on paper
90460.e: Pseudocode has no fixed rules that a computer could understand. That is why you first translate it, for example, into Python or Scratch.
90460.m: Pseudocode is written for people and has to be translated first for the computer.

90461.q: Why do people often write pseudocode before they program?
a: To plan the steps without worrying about the exact way of writing them
So that the program runs faster
So that nobody can read the program
90461.e: With pseudocode you can first concentrate on the idea of the algorithm. The exact rules of the programming language only come afterwards.
90461.m: With pseudocode you plan the idea first and the exact code afterwards.

90462.q: Pseudocode: x ← 5, then x ← x + 3, then OUTPUT x. What is output?
90462.e: First x gets the value 5. Then 3 is added, so x = 8.
90462.m: In an assignment, the new value is calculated from the old value and stored.

90463.q: What does the arrow ← mean in many pseudocodes, for example in “points ← 0”?
a: A value is assigned to the variable
Something is drawn to the left
90463.e: The arrow stands for an assignment: the variable “points” gets the value 0. In Python you write points = 0.
90463.m: The arrow in pseudocode stands for an assignment to a variable.

90464.q: Pseudocode: sum ← 0, then FOR i FROM 1 TO 4: sum ← sum + i, then OUTPUT sum. What is output?
90464.e: The loop adds up 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. That gives 10.
90464.m: With a counting loop you can add up many numbers one after another.

90465.q: Pseudocode: number ← 7. IF number MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT “even” ELSE OUTPUT “odd”. What is output?
90465.e: MOD 2 gives the remainder when dividing by 2. For 7 the remainder is 1, so the condition is false and the ELSE part is carried out.
90465.m: With the remainder when dividing by 2 you can tell even and odd numbers apart.

90466.q: Pseudocode: a ← 3, b ← 5, then a ← b, then b ← a. What values do a and b have at the end?
90466.e: After a ← b, a = 5 and the old value 3 is lost. Then b gets the value of a, so 5 again.
90466.m: To swap two variables you usually need a helper variable.

90467.q: Pseudocode: x ← 3. WHILE x < 20: x ← x · 2. Then OUTPUT x. What is output?
90467.e: x is doubled: 3, 6, 12, 24. At 24 the condition x < 20 is false, so the loop ends.
90467.m: A while loop checks its condition before every run.

a: To show the steps of a program clearly
90468.e: A structogram uses blocks to show which steps a program carries out in sequence, in branches and in loops. It is also called a Nassi-Shneiderman diagram after its inventors.
90468.m: A structogram shows the steps of a program.

90469.q: Which other diagram also shows the steps of a program graphically, but with arrows?
90469.e: Structograms and flowcharts both show the steps of programs. The flowchart connects the steps with arrows, the structogram stacks blocks.
90469.m: Structograms and flowcharts show the steps of programs.

90470.q: Which basic shapes is a structogram made of?
a: Rectangles placed one below the other
90470.e: A structogram consists of rectangular blocks. The instructions are carried out in order from top to bottom.
90470.m: A structogram consists of rectangular blocks that you read from top to bottom.

90471.q: What is there not in a structogram, unlike in a flowchart?
a: Arrows that jump back and forth anywhere
90471.e: In a structogram the order is fixed by the arrangement of the blocks. Jumps anywhere, as in a flowchart, are not possible.

90472.q: How is a branch (if, then, else) shown in a structogram?
a: With a triangle at the top and two columns for yes and no
With a circle in the middle
90472.e: At the top is the condition in a field with triangles. Below it the block divides into a yes column and a no column.
90472.m: A branch in a structogram divides into a yes column and a no column.

90473.q: How do you recognise a loop in a structogram?
a: A block encloses the repeated instructions from the left
Two blocks stand side by side
90473.e: In a loop the condition is at the top, and a wide border encloses the instructions that are repeated. This shows what belongs to the loop.
90473.m: In a structogram the loop block encloses all the repeated instructions.

90474.q: A structogram contains: number ← 4, then “repeat 3 times: number ← number + 2”, then “output number”. What is output?
90474.e: The number starts at 4 and is increased by 2 three times: 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10.
90474.m: The blocks of a structogram are worked through in order.

90475.q: What are instructions called that simply stand one below the other in a structogram and are carried out one after another?
90475.e: A sequence is a series of instructions without a condition. It is carried out exactly once from top to bottom.
90475.m: A sequence is a series of instructions that are carried out one after another.

90476.q: Why is bubble sort called that?
a: Large values rise like bubbles to the end
It was invented by Mr Bubble
90476.e: In every pass, the large values move step by step towards the end, like rising air bubbles.
90476.m: In bubble sort the large values rise like bubbles to the end of the list.

90477.q: How many comparisons does bubble sort make in one pass through a list of 6 numbers?
90477.e: Two neighbours are always compared: place 1 with 2, 2 with 3 and so on up to 5 with 6. That makes 5 comparisons.
90477.m: With n numbers, bubble sort makes n minus 1 comparisons per pass.

90478.q: When can bubble sort stop sorting early?
a: When nothing was swapped in a pass
When the first number is a 1
When the list has an even number of numbers
90478.e: If there is no swap in a whole pass, the list is already sorted. More passes are then not needed.
90478.m: If there is no swap in a pass, the list is fully sorted.

90479.q: Bubble sort sorts the list 3, 2, 1 in ascending order. How many swaps are needed in total?
90479.e: 3, 2, 1 becomes 2, 3, 1 and then 2, 1, 3. In the second pass 2, 1, 3 becomes 1, 2, 3. That makes 3 swaps.
90479.m: The more jumbled a list is, the more bubble sort has to swap.

90480.q: What is the maximum number of passes bubble sort needs for 5 numbers so that the list is definitely sorted?
90480.e: After every pass at least one more number is in the right place. With 5 numbers, 4 passes are enough, because then the last one is in the right place too.
90480.m: With n numbers, bubble sort needs at most n minus 1 passes.

90481.q: How many comparisons does bubble sort make in total for 4 numbers if it does all the passes and leaves out the finished part at the end each time?
90481.e: The first pass needs 3 comparisons, the second 2 and the third 1. Together that makes 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
90481.m: Bubble sort compares one pair fewer in every pass.

90482.q: Why is bubble sort hardly ever used for very large amounts of data?
a: It needs a great many comparisons and swaps
It only sorts in descending order
90482.e: With twice as many numbers, bubble sort needs about four times as many comparisons. For large lists there are much faster methods.
90482.m: Bubble sort is easy to understand, but too slow for large lists.

90483.q: How many swaps does bubble sort make with the already sorted list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
90483.e: All neighbours are already in the right order. That is why nothing is swapped.
90483.m: An already sorted list needs no swaps.

90484.q: What is always true of the front part of the list in insertion sort?
90484.e: Insertion sort builds up a sorted part of the list at the front step by step. Each new element is inserted there in the right place.
90484.m: In insertion sort a sorted part grows at the front of the list.

90485.q: The sorted part is 2, 5, 7. Where does insertion sort insert the number 4 next?
90485.e: 4 is greater than 2 but smaller than 5. So it belongs between 2 and 5, giving 2, 4, 5, 7.
90485.m: Insertion sort inserts every new element exactly in the right place.

90486.q: Insertion sort sorts the list 4, 3, 1, 2. What does the list look like after the first two numbers are sorted?
90486.e: The 3 is inserted before the 4. The numbers 1 and 2 have not been dealt with yet and stay where they are.
90486.m: Insertion sort deals with the numbers in order from front to back.

90487.q: For which list does insertion sort work especially fast?
a: For a list sorted in reverse
For a list with only negative numbers
For a list with very large numbers
90487.e: If the list is almost sorted, hardly any element has to be moved far. Then insertion sort needs only a few steps.
90487.m: Insertion sort is very fast with almost sorted lists.

90488.q: For which starting list does insertion sort have to work the hardest?
a: For a list sorted in reverse
For a list of identical numbers
For a list with two numbers
90488.e: If the list is sorted in reverse, every new element has to move right to the front. This needs the most comparisons and moves.
90488.m: A list sorted in reverse is the worst case for insertion sort.

90489.q: How many comparisons does insertion sort need for the already sorted list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6?
90489.e: Every element from the second onwards is compared only once with its left neighbour and then stays put. That makes 5 comparisons.
90489.m: With a sorted list, insertion sort needs only one comparison per element.

90490.q: Insertion sort works like sorting playing cards in your hand. What do you do with each new card?
a: You slot it in at the right place
You always put it right at the back
You shuffle all the cards again
You swap it with the first card
90490.e: You compare the new card with the cards already sorted and slot it in where it belongs. That is exactly how insertion sort works.
90490.m: Insertion sort sorts like arranging playing cards.

90491.q: Does insertion sort need a second list of the same size as temporary storage?
a: No, it sorts directly in the existing list
90491.e: Insertion sort moves the elements within the existing list. This is called “in-place”; it needs only very little extra memory.
90491.m: Insertion sort sorts directly in the list and so saves memory.

90492.q: Roughly what share of the list is left after each comparison in a binary search?
90492.e: Binary search compares with the middle element and then rules out one half. This halves the search area with every step.
90492.m: Binary search halves the search area with every comparison.

90493.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs in a sorted list of 1000 entries?
90493.e: You can halve 1000 at most about ten times until only one entry is left, because 2 to the power of 10 is 1024. That is why 10 comparisons are enough.
90493.m: With 10 halvings you can find one entry among 1000.

90494.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs in a sorted list of one million entries?
90494.e: 2 to the power of 20 is a little more than a million. That is why 20 halvings are enough to find any entry.
90494.m: Even with a million entries, binary search needs only about 20 comparisons.

90495.q: A sorted list becomes twice as long. How many more comparisons does binary search need at most?
90495.e: One extra comparison halves the list that is twice as long back to the old length. After that everything works as before.
90495.m: A list twice as long costs binary search only one more comparison.

90496.q: Binary search looks for 7 in the list 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 29. After how many comparisons is the 7 found?
90496.e: First it compares with the middle, 15; 7 is smaller. In the left part 3, 7, 11 the middle is 7, so it is found after the second comparison.
90496.m: Binary search always jumps to the middle of the remaining area.

90497.q: The number you are looking for is smaller than the middle element of a list sorted in ascending order. Where does binary search continue?
90497.e: In a list sorted in ascending order the smaller numbers are at the front. So the back half can be ruled out.
90497.m: If the value you want is smaller than the middle, you keep searching at the front.

90498.q: How does binary search know that the number it is looking for is not in the list?
a: The first number is a zero
The middle is always the same
90498.e: With every comparison the search area shrinks. If it is empty and the number has not been found, it is not in the list.
90498.m: An empty search area means the value is missing.

90499.q: Which element does binary search compare the value it is looking for with at each step?
a: With the middle element of the search area
With the first element of the list
With the last element of the list
90499.e: The middle element splits the area into two halves of the same size. This lets you rule out half with one comparison.
90499.m: Binary search always compares with the middle of the search area.

90500.q: Which well-known algorithm finds the shortest path from a starting point in a network with distances?
90500.e: Starting from a start node, Dijkstra's algorithm gradually examines the nearest nodes. In this way it finds the shortest paths to all destinations.
90500.m: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in a network.

90501.q: A satnav is meant to find the fastest route, not the shortest. Which number does it then need for each road?
90501.e: For the fastest route, what matters is how long each section takes. A short road with a traffic jam can be slower than a detour.
90501.m: For the fastest route you calculate with travel times.

90502.q: Where are shortest-path algorithms often used in everyday life?
a: In navigation apps and route planners
90502.e: Navigation apps represent roads as a network with lengths or travel times. In it they look for the shortest or fastest route.
90502.m: Route planners use algorithms to find the shortest route.

90503.q: Routes: A to B 4 km, B to C 3 km, A to C 9 km, C to D 2 km, B to D 8 km. How long is the shortest route from A to D?
90503.e: A, B, C, D gives 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 km. A, C, D gives 11 km and A, B, D gives 12 km.
90503.m: To find the shortest route you compare the total distances of all possible routes.

90504.q: What does the weight of an edge tell you when searching for the shortest path?
a: How long or costly that connection is
90504.e: The edge weight can be a distance, a travel time or a price. The shortest path has the smallest total of weights.
90504.m: For the shortest path, what counts is the total of the edge weights.

90505.q: Is the route with the fewest edges always the shortest route?
a: No, what matters is the total of the weights
No, the longest route is always the fastest
90505.e: A detour over several short connections can be shorter than a single long connection. It is only always true if all edges are the same length.
90505.m: Several sections together can still be shorter than a single long one.

90506.q: In a network, every connection counts the same. Which route is then the shortest?
a: The route with the fewest connections
The route with the most connections
The route that was drawn first
The route via the largest node
90506.e: If all connections are the same length, you only count the steps. The fewer connections, the shorter the route.
90506.m: If all connections are the same length, the route with the fewest steps wins.

90507.q: Routes: A to B 2 km, B to C 2 km, A to C 5 km. How long is the shortest route from A to C?
90507.e: Via B it is 2 + 2 = 4 km. The direct route, at 5 km, is longer.
90507.m: A detour can be shorter than the direct route.

90508.q: A satnav learns about a traffic jam on the planned route. What is the sensible thing for it to do?
a: It looks for a new route with a shorter travel time
It drives through the jam anyway
It no longer shows a route
It always chooses the longest route
90508.e: The jam increases the travel time on this route. The satnav recalculates the fastest route with the new values.
90508.m: If travel times change, the satnav recalculates the route.

90509.q: A railway network is shown as a graph. What are the nodes?
90509.e: Nodes are the points of a graph, here the stations. The connections between them are the edges.
90509.m: In a graph, places are the nodes and connections are the edges.

90510.q: In a graph, the people in a class are the nodes. What could the edges be?
90510.e: An edge always connects two nodes. A friendship between two people is therefore a suitable edge.
90510.m: An edge always connects two nodes with each other.

90511.q: Which kind of graph do you need for a road network with one-way streets?
90511.e: In a directed graph every edge has a direction, like an arrow. This lets you show that a road can only be driven in one direction.
90511.m: Directed graphs have edges with a fixed direction.

90512.q: What is a graph called in which every edge carries a number such as a distance?
90512.e: The numbers on the edges are called weights. They can give, for example, kilometres, minutes or costs.
90512.m: In a weighted graph every edge carries a number.

90513.q: A node is connected by edges to 4 other nodes. What degree does this node have?
90513.e: The degree of a node is the number of edges that end at it. Here there are 4.
90513.m: The degree of a node counts its edges.

90514.q: 5 people all shake hands with each other once. How many edges does the matching graph have?
90514.e: Each of the 5 people shakes hands with 4 others, which gives 5 · 4 = 20. Because every handshake was counted twice, it is 20 : 2 = 10.
90514.m: In handshake problems you may only count each handshake once.

90515.q: What is a connected graph that contains no cycles called?
90515.e: In a tree there is always exactly one path between two nodes. Folder structures on a computer, for example, have this shape.
90515.m: A tree is a connected graph without cycles.

90516.q: What does it mean that a graph is connected?
a: From every node you can get to every other node via edges
All nodes have the same number of edges
Every node is directly connected to every other
90516.e: In a connected graph there is a path between any two nodes. This path may also lead via other nodes.
90516.m: In a connected graph every node can be reached from every other.

90517.q: What does decomposition mean in problem solving?
a: Splitting a big problem into smaller sub-problems
Passing a problem on to someone else
Copying out a problem several times
90517.e: Smaller sub-problems are clearer and easier to solve. Put together, their solutions give the solution to the whole problem.
90517.m: You solve big problems by breaking them down into small sub-problems.

90518.q: You want to program a game. What is decomposition?
a: Splitting the task into parts such as character, controls and points
Writing the whole game in one step
90518.e: Instead of solving everything at once, you split the game into small parts. Each part is simpler and can be programmed and tested separately.
90518.m: Breaking a problem down into parts is called decomposition.

90519.q: Which division is a sensible decomposition for planning a class party?
a: Invitations, food, games and tidying up
90519.e: Each of these sub-tasks can be planned and done on its own. Together they make up the whole party.
90519.m: A good decomposition gives sub-tasks that you can do separately.

90520.q: How are sub-problems often put into practice when programming?
90520.e: You write a separate function for each sub-problem. The main program then calls these functions in order.
90520.m: When programming, sub-problems often become separate functions.

90521.q: What advantage is there when a team breaks a program down into sub-problems?
a: Different people can work on parts at the same time
The program no longer needs electricity
90521.e: If the parts are clearly separated, each person can work on one part. Afterwards the parts are put together and tested together.
90521.m: Decomposition lets a team work on different parts at the same time.

90522.q: What is the approach called in which you start from the whole problem and break it down into finer and finer parts?
90522.e: With top-down you start at the top with the whole and refine it step by step. With bottom-up, on the other hand, you put small parts together into something bigger.
90522.m: Top-down means working from the whole to the details.

90523.q: When do you not need to break a sub-problem down any further?
a: When you can solve it directly
When it has more than three words
When it is at the end of the list
When it is already a week old
90523.e: Decomposition stops as soon as a sub-problem is simple enough to solve directly. Breaking it down further would only create work.
90523.m: You keep breaking things down until every sub-problem can be solved directly.

90524.q: A quiz program is to be programmed. Which is a sensible sub-problem?
a: Checking the answer and counting points
90524.e: Checking the answer and counting the points is a clearly separate part of the program. The other tasks have nothing to do with the program itself.
90524.m: A sub-problem is a clearly separate part of the actual task.

90525.q: What does abstraction mean in computing?
a: Leaving out unimportant details and keeping what matters
Making a program as complicated as possible
90525.e: With abstraction you concentrate on what is important for the task. Everything else you leave out on purpose.
90525.m: Abstraction means keeping what matters and leaving out what does not.

90526.q: Which map is a good example of abstraction?
a: A bus and tram network map
An aerial photo of the whole city
A video of a tram ride
90526.e: The network map only shows stops and lines, not the exact distances or buildings. That is enough to find the right connection.
90526.m: A network map only shows what you need for the journey.

90527.q: What is a simplified picture of reality that contains only the important features called?
90527.e: A model leaves out details on purpose. This makes it easier to understand a problem or calculate it with a computer.
90527.m: A model is a simplified picture of reality.

90528.q: You are planning a bike tour with a program. Which information is most important for this?
a: Distance and climb of the route
Colour of the houses along the way
Number of windows in the station
90528.e: For a bike tour, what mainly counts is the length and steepness of the route. The program can leave out the other details.
90528.m: Good abstraction keeps only the information that is needed for the task.

90529.q: You call print() in Python without knowing how the output works inside. What is this an example of?
90529.e: The function print() hides the complicated details. You only need to know what it does, not how it does it.
90529.m: Functions hide details and are therefore a form of abstraction.

90530.q: What is the part called through which you operate a device or program without knowing its inner workings?
90530.e: An interface sets out how you use something. In a car, for example, that is the steering wheel and pedals; you do not need to understand the engine.
90530.m: Through an interface you use something without knowing its inner workings.

90531.q: A turtle program is to draw any regular polygon with n corners. By how many degrees does the turtle turn after each side?
90531.e: After all n turns, the turtle has turned all the way round once, so by 360 degrees. With 6 corners, for example, that is 360 : 6 = 60 degrees.
90531.m: A program with a parameter solves many similar tasks at once.

90532.q: A game stores only the position, health points and equipment of a character. Which way of thinking is behind this?
90532.e: The game stores only what is needed for playing. All other details are left out on purpose.
90532.m: Through abstraction, programs store only the properties they need.

90533.q: What does pattern recognition mean in computational thinking?
a: Finding similarities and repetitions in problems
90533.e: If you notice that something repeats or is similar to a known problem, you can reuse known solutions. This saves time and work.
90533.m: Pattern recognition helps you reuse known solutions.

90534.e: Each number is three times as big as the one before. 54 · 3 = 162.
90534.m: In some sequences each number is multiplied by the same factor.

90535.e: Each number is doubled and then reduced by 1: 33 · 2 = 66, and 66 minus 1 is 65. You can also see it from the gaps 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, which double.
90535.m: If you look at the gaps in a sequence, you can often see the pattern.

90536.q: How does the letter sequence A, C, E, G, ... continue?
90536.e: One letter is skipped each time. So after G comes I.
90536.m: With letters, too, you can find patterns with fixed gaps.

90537.q: For 1 square made of matches you need 4 matches, for 2 squares in a row 7, for 3 squares 10. How many matches do you need for 10 squares in a row?
90537.e: Each extra square adds 3 matches. So you need 4 + 9 · 3 = 31 matches.
90537.m: If you recognise the pattern, you can work out large cases without a drawing.

90538.q: In a program, the same two commands appear eight times in a row. How can you simplify this?
90538.e: You spot the pattern of repetition and put the two commands into a loop that runs eight times. The program becomes shorter and clearer.
90538.m: You group repeated commands together in a loop.

90539.q: How does a spam filter recognise unwanted emails?
a: By typical patterns it has learnt from many example emails
It reads every email aloud to a person
It deletes all emails with pictures
It blocks all emails at the weekend
90539.e: Spam filters compare new emails with the features of known spam emails, for example certain words or senders. If the pattern matches, the email goes into the spam folder.
90539.m: Spam filters recognise unwanted emails by typical patterns.

90540.q: Which kind of pattern recognition do many smartphones use to unlock the screen?
90540.e: The phone compares the features of the face with stored data. If the pattern matches, the screen is unlocked.
90540.m: With face recognition the phone compares facial features with stored data.

90541.e: These are the square numbers 1 · 1, 2 · 2, 3 · 3 and so on. Next comes 6 · 6 = 36.
90541.m: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself.

90542.q: What is a common cause of an unintended infinite loop?
a: The variable in the condition is never changed in the loop
The program has too many comments
The variable has a long name
90542.e: If the variable in the condition never changes, the condition stays true for ever. Then the loop keeps running without end.
90542.m: A loop only ends if its condition changes at some point.

90543.q: Pseudocode: i ← 10. WHILE i ≠ 0: i ← i − 3. Why does this loop never end?
a: The condition is false from the start
90543.e: i takes the values 10, 7, 4, 1, -2, -5 and so on. It never hits 0 exactly, so the condition always stays true.
90543.m: A condition with “not equal to” can lead to an infinite loop if the value is skipped.

90544.q: Which Scratch block is deliberately an infinite loop?
90544.e: The “forever” block repeats its contents until the program is stopped. It is often used for games and animations.
90544.m: In Scratch, “forever” creates an intended infinite loop.

90545.q: Where is an infinite loop often intended?
90545.e: Traffic light control is meant to run through the same phases again and again as long as the system is switched on. An infinite loop makes sense for this.
90545.m: Control systems that are meant to run all the time use intended infinite loops.

90546.q: Which key combination usually stops a program that has hung in a console?
90546.e: In the console, Ctrl + C sends a stop signal to the running program. This lets you stop an infinite loop.
90546.m: In the console, Ctrl + C stops a running program.

90547.q: How can you often tell that a program is stuck in an infinite loop?
a: It stops responding and never finishes
It shows the right result straight away
90547.e: The program keeps calculating without end and never gets to the next step. Often it no longer responds to input.
90547.m: A program in an infinite loop never finishes.

90548.q: Can a program reliably predict for any other program whether it will run for ever?
a: No, Alan Turing proved this in 1936
90548.e: This question is called the halting problem. Alan Turing showed that there cannot be a program that answers it correctly for all programs.
90548.m: There is no program that can tell for every program whether it runs for ever.

90549.q: Which of these loops is an infinite loop (x starts at 1)?
90549.e: If x keeps getting bigger, x > 0 stays true for ever. In the other loops the condition becomes false after a few runs.
90549.m: A loop runs for ever if the variable moves away from the stopping condition.

90550.q: When programming a game, what is the “game loop”?
a: An intended infinite loop that reads input and redraws the picture
An error that makes the game crash
90550.e: The game loop runs through again and again during the whole game. In every run it processes input, moves characters and draws the picture.
90550.m: Games run in a game loop that repeats all the time.

90551.q: What does the running time of an algorithm describe?
a: How many steps or how much time it needs
How many lines the code has
How long the computer has been running
90551.e: The running time tells you how much work an algorithm takes. What matters most is how much it grows with larger inputs.
90551.m: The running time measures how much work an algorithm needs.

90552.q: Why do people often count calculation steps rather than seconds for running time?
a: Because computers do not know about time
90552.e: The same algorithm runs in fewer seconds on a fast computer. But the number of steps stays the same and is easier to compare.
90552.m: Calculation steps make algorithms comparable regardless of the computer.

90553.q: A list becomes twice as long. How does the number of comparisons in a linear search change in the worst case?
a: It becomes four times as big
It only goes up by one
90553.e: In the worst case, linear search checks every element once. Twice as many elements means twice as many comparisons.
90553.m: With linear running time, the work grows at the same rate as the input.

90554.q: A loop runs n times, and inside it a second loop also runs n times. How often is the inner part carried out when n = 20?
90554.e: For each of the 20 outer runs, the inner loop runs 20 times. That gives 20 · 20 = 400.
90554.m: Nested loops multiply the number of runs.

90555.q: What is the case called in which an algorithm needs the most steps?
90555.e: The worst case tells you the longest an algorithm can take. That way you know what you can rely on.
90555.m: The worst case shows the greatest possible work for an algorithm.
